name: Aiglon College
title: UVitis: Improving the Vitality of Grapes
abstract:
In Vaud, high-altitude vineyards face UV indices reaching 9, causing heat damage, altered sugar and acid ratios, and undesirable aromas that threaten wine quality. While kaolin clay particle films reflect sunlight to reduce heat stress, it is easily washed off by rain. 

Project UVitis engineers a fusion protein that functions as biological double-sided tape, anchoring kaolin particles to grape waxy cuticles. The construct joins a silica/kaolin-binding peptide (Car9, SB7, or R5), a flexible linker, an sfGFP fluorescent reporter, and MacHis, a plant-wax-binding peptide. Expressed in non-pathogenic E. coli, the presence of the fusion proteins were evaluated through fluorescence. 

Therefore, through enhancing kaolin retention, UVitis offers a more sustainable bio-shield to protect viticulture against climate stressors.

name: Alicante University
title: 1,3-Dimethoxybenzene: An insight on fungal compounds against nematodes
abstract: Plant-parasitic nematodes cause major crop losses worldwide. The fungus Pochonia chlamydosporia naturally produces 1,3-dimethoxybenzene (C5), a volatile compound with nematicidal activity, but its biosynthetic pathway remains uncharacterised. NemaVOC aims to reconstruct and optimise this pathway in Escherichia coli using genes from other organisms encoding a polyketide synthase (PKS), a decarboxylase and an O-methyltransferase (OMT). Plasmid constructs with codon-optimised sequences under constitutive promoters will be assembled following a modular approach: each enzyme is first tested individually, then combined to rebuild the full pathway, aiming for a strain that produces C5 from simple precursors and ultimately from glucose. We will assess C5 toxicity on E. coli, study C5 production by P. chlamydosporia strain Pc123 under different culture conditions including resorcinol supplementation, and begin with heterologous OMT expression using resorcinol as substrate. Molecular modelling and docking will explore C5 interactions with nematode target proteins.

name: BIT-China
title: HERBAL——Herb Evaluation via Rapid Bacterial Assay for Licorice
abstract: Herbal materials can look similar yet differ substantially in their bioactive constituents. HERBAL aims to make compositional screening more accessible, using licorice as its first application. Our design combines enzymatic pretreatment with engineered yeast and Escherichia coli to sense glycyrrhetinic acid, liquiritigenin, and selected phenolic acids. We investigate two routes: direct fluorescence readout for practical screening and molecular communication with the computing strain to explore biological information processing. A compact reader integrates mixing, temperature control, and optical detection, while calibration and modeling connect fluorescence to concentration estimates.  We also developed BIO-NET, an open-source platform for biological network design and simulation. Guided by growers, traders, and testing specialists, HERBAL prioritizes batch comparison during purchasing, aiming to support better-informed decisions and future applications in other herbal materials.

name: BJWZ-China
title: Tree Guard: Engineered Bacillus subtilis with LysM₃‑ChiA and RNAi Against Peach Gummosis
abstract: To address the challenge that Botryosphaeria dothidea conceals chitin via the LysM domain of its BdLM1 protein to evade peach PTI (PAMP‑Triggered Immunity), we constructed a dual‑action biocontrol system using engineered Bacillus subtilis. The engineered strain continuously secretes the LysM₃‑Cat fusion protein, which competitively masks pathogen cell‑wall chitin through high‑affinity multivalent LysM binding, thereby blocking immune evasion. Concurrently, the GH18 catalytic domain specifically hydrolyzes chitin at hyphal tips, releasing chitin oligosaccharides (DAMPs) that activate plant PTI immunity. Furthermore, we designed siRNA targeting the BdLM1 gene to silence its expression, abolishing the pathogen's immune‑suppressive strategy and restoring the tree's defense. Upon colonization in peach trees, this system achieves triple synergy: direct antifungal killing, immunity activation, and immune restoration. Laboratory validation confirms that this strategy efficiently inhibits hyphal growth and substantially reduces reliance on chemical pesticides, providing a green, long‑lasting synthetic‑biology solution for peach gummosis management.

name: BWYA
title: Flowever
abstract: Cut flowers have a limited vase life, leading to premature disposal and resource waste. Flowever aims to develop a sustainable flower preservative using melatonin produced through synthetic biology. We engineered Escherichia coli with an optimized nine-gene biosynthetic pathway, achieving a melatonin concentration of 159.02 mg/L after 96 hours. To reduce purification costs and improve stability, we developed a preservative combining filtered fermentation supernatant with citric acid. In laboratory trials, our formulation delayed visual deterioration in carnations. In one experiment, all treated carnations retained ornamental value on Day 6, while none in the water control did. Guided by stakeholder interviews and consumer research, we explored commercial applications in hotels and commercial complexes. Flowever connects synthetic biology with practical flower preservation, aiming to extend flower longevity and reduce waste.

name: CCA-SanDiego
title: PestiSense
abstract: Pesticide contamination threatens public health through potential neurotoxicity and associations with neurodegenerative diseases. However, conventional detection requires expensive equipment and time-consuming procedures, limiting on-site testing. Our project developed and experimentally evaluated a cell-free fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based aptasensor for detecting rotenone and malathion. The system comprises a fluorophore-labeled DNA aptamer (FDNA) and a complementary quencher-labeled strand (QDNA). In the absence of pesticide, hybridization suppresses fluorescence. Target binding is expected to separate the fluorophore and quencher, restoring fluorescence. Two aptamer candidates, AX12 targeting rotenone and MalR targeting malathion, were designed and evaluated alongside existing candidates. Quenching assays showed reduced fluorescence with increasing QDNA concentrations, supporting proper quenching. Pesticide-response experiments demonstrated generally increasing fluorescence across the tested concentration ranges, indicating promising pesticide targeting despite some experimental variability. These preliminary findings establish a foundation for further development. Future work will validate binding independently, improve reproducibility, assess selectivity, and determine detection limits.

name: CCU-Taiwan
title: NoFold: Engineering E. coli to Produce L-Limonene Against the Rice Leafroller
abstract: The rice leafroller (Cnaphalocrocis medinalis) is a migratory pest that damages rice across East Asia, and farmers rely heavily on chemical pesticides to control it. NoFold engineers Escherichia coli to produce L-limonene, a plant terpene reported to repel the rice leafroller and reduce its egg-laying. The limonene is extracted from the culture and applied as a spray, so no engineered cells are released into the field. Our strain expresses a geranyl diphosphate synthase and a limonene synthase, and we pursue two strategies to raise yield: overexpressing DXS and IDI to increase precursor supply through the native MEP pathway, and fusing the two final enzymes to bring their active sites closer together. We complemented the wet-lab design with metabolic and molecular modeling, consulted agricultural stakeholders, and ran outreach on sustainable farming. NoFold aims to give rice farmers a bio-based alternative to chemical pesticides.

name: City-of-London-UK
title: Vinalysis - A Rapid Test for Smoke-tainted Grapes
abstract:
As climate change increases the occurrence and scale of wildfires, smoke taint is costing the global wine industry hundreds of millions every year. Volatile phenols are carried vast distances by wildfire smoke and bind to sugars in grapes undetectably. Fermentation of tainted grapes to produce wine releases these phenols, which have a strong smoky and medicinal flavour, rendering the wine unsellable. Current lab tests for smoke taint are expensive and take weeks, leaving a costly waiting period right before harvest. 

Vinalysis is an affordable, rapid triage test for use in the vineyard, which quantifies the concentrations of two common phenols: guaiacol and syringol. After enzymatic cleavage frees these compounds, guaiacol will bind to a guaiacol-binding aptamer in an RNA riboswitch, and syringol will cause the transcription factor DesX to undergo a shape change. This will result in the production of fluorescence via GFP, indicating the degree of smoke taint.

name: CUHK-Shenzhen
title: Plant SOS: A plant hormone biosensor complex for early warning of biotic and abiotic stresses
abstract: 3 critical hormones SA, JA, ABA play important roles in regulating plant growth and coping with biotic and abiotic stress. We design a stress onset sensor complex called Plant SOS. We aim to realize an detection system including SA, JA, ABA sensors and estimate the amount of different plant hormones via luminescence intensity. And we will also construct a model for interactive analysis of fluctuations across three hormones. Through this biosensor complex we can evaluate the state of plants more efficiently, economically, comprehensively than traditional methods, and give valuable advises in early disease prevention.

name: ECUST
title: The Great Wall: Engineering Light-Programmable Living Microrobots for Precision Mucosal Vaccination in Aquaculture
abstract: Immersion vaccination offers scalable protection for juvenile fish, yet the mucosal barrier limits antigen delivery. Building on our previous Wukong project, The Great Wall shifts to LOV–CheZ fusions designed for direct, protein-level regulation of bacterial motility. Through iterative DBTL cycles, we constructed three variants; the best candidate produced larger swimming halos under blue light than in darkness in soft-agar assays. To quantify motility and explore delivery, we developed bacterial tracking software and an agent-based model. Model simulations predicted 42.7% greater antigen transport across the mucosal barrier within five minutes under pulsed illumination than without illumination. We also developed a biomimetic microfluidic chip and integrated an illuminated screw immersion device with a smart vaccine workstation, achieving 95% vaccine utilization in controlled recirculation. Guided by stakeholder input and adhering to approved animal-use and biosafety protocols, this contained platform advances light-controlled mucosal delivery toward practical, environmentally responsible aquaculture vaccination.

name: GeorgiaState
title: REDAlert: Engineering an Early Visual Warning System for Rice Blast Disease
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, is among the most destructive rice diseases, yet farmers usually notice symptoms only after preventive fungicide is no longer effective. REDAlert (Riceblast Early Detection Alert) is a synthetic biology system designed to make rice visibly signal infection before symptoms appear, giving smallholder farmers time to act. A chimeric receptor fusing the OsTPR1 ectodomain to OsCERK1 transmembrane and kinase domains detects MoChia1, an effector the fungus secretes to mask its chitin. Binding prompts the 14-3-3 adapter OsGF14f to recruit split-TEV protease, releasing GAL4-VP16 to drive RUBY betalain production, a red pigment readable without lab equipment. This season we validated protoplast isolation and are testing the circuit by PEG-mediated transfection of rice protoplasts, supported by structural modeling and design decisions shaped by regulators, industry scientists, researchers, ethicists, and farmers.

name: Guelph
title: Lumifert
abstract: Conventional synthetic fertilizers are unsustainable due to energy-intensive production, supply chain volatility, and ineffective nutrient release, resulting in financial losses for farmers and environmental destruction. The objective of this research is to develop a bioengineered slow-release fertilizer with tunable nutrient content that can be produced onsite at farming operations. The fertilizer biomass is composed of a consortium of duckweed (Lemna minor) and bacteria (Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus) genetically engineered to accumulate phosphorous and nitrogen under optogenetic regulation. This work establishes a proof-of-concept for an optogenetically regulated plant-microbe fertilizer platform that could reduce reliance on conventional synthetic fertilizers and achieve comparable macronutrient delivery while reducing greenhouse gas emissions and runoff. This project is informed by ongoing consultations with stakeholders, academics, and industry professionals to ensure it is technically and commercially viable. Commercialization of the developed fertilizer would support the sustainable intensification of agriculture in alignment with global food security and climate mitigation goals.

name: HainanU-YZ-China
title: GreenShield MicroControl · miRNA Biopesticide
abstract:
Gray mold seriously reduces tomato yield and quality in protected cultivation. Conventional chemical pesticides cause pesticide residues and pathogen resistance, while traditional dsRNA agents are costly, single-functional and easily degraded, limiting field application. We adopt tomato endogenous miR393 as the core factor to develop eco-friendly biopesticides.
 
miR393 exhibits dual functions: it enters Botrytis cinerea cells to inhibit cell wall synthesis and block infection; meanwhile, it triggers tomato PTI basal defense via JA/SA pathways to strengthen plant immunity. We use E. coli HT115 for prokaryotic expression and construct SPc and low-cost quaternized chitosan delivery systems. Seedling tests confirm good biosafety. We build an induction kinetic model for our fermentation optimization and a Hill‑XGBoost model offering universal references for global researchers. This work provides a green strategy for gray mold control and advances endogenous small RNA biopesticides.

name: HIA-Taiwan
title: AiyUReady: A Methanol-Based Biosensor for Aiyu Ripeness and Gel Quality
abstract:
Taiwan produces approximately 700 metric tons of Aiyu annually, yet harvest decisions rely largely on farmers’ visual judgment and experience. Premature harvesting can compromise gel formation and product quality. AiyUReady investigates methanol, released during pectin demethylation, as a potential indicator of Aiyu quality.
We designed a two-plasmid biosensor in Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655. The upstream module expresses methanol dehydrogenase to convert methanol into formaldehyde, while the downstream module uses a formaldehyde-responsive promoter to drive AmilCP expression, producing a blue-purple signal. Mathematical modeling connects enzyme expression, formaldehyde production, cellular detoxification, and reporter output to guide construct design.
Farmer consultations informed our proposed application, emphasizing affordability, clear interpretation, and compatibility with farming experience. Educational outreach connected synthetic biology with local agriculture and Taiwanese food culture.
Further calibration against methanol concentration and gel performance, followed by field validation, is needed to determine whether AiyUReady can provide a reliable additional reference for harvest decisions.

name: HongKong-JSS
title: MerMAID: MerR-based Mercury Assay for In-field Detection
abstract: Mercury is a potent, bioaccumulative neurotoxin that threatens Hong Kong's agriculture on two fronts. In local farmland, the historical use of mercury-containing agrochemicals has left elevated mercury in agricultural soils. In mariculture, mercury bioaccumulates up the food chain into farmed fish—a dietary staple—raising the burden on local consumers. Yet on-site monitoring stays costly and lab-dependent. We present a MerR-based biosensor for in-field detection, coupling the mercury-responsive merR/pMer element to the reporter mRFP1e for dual readouts: visible colour for equipment-free early warning, and fluorescence for precise quantification. After screening over ten protein-based variants, we optimised one construct showing a reliable dose-response, broad dynamic range, and a detection limit below WHO standards. We validated it in mercury-spiked garden-soil matrices and showed that alginate-bead encapsulation preserves function—enhancing field use and biosafety.

name: HSET-China
title: Silicon Shield: A synthetic biology platform that enhances crop stress resistance using plant silicon transporters
abstract: This project uses Nicotiana benthamiana as a model plant for verification and constructs an efficient artificial gene pathway for silicon absorption, transport, and deposition based on the standardized approach of synthetic biology. By heterologously expressing highly active silicon transporter proteins from plants, the project enhances tobacco's ability to enrich silicon in soil/water and deposit it in cell walls. Utilizing the physical reinforcement, antioxidant, and osmotic stress resistance properties of silicon, the project aims to achieve multi-dimensional enhancement of crop resistance to drought, salt, high temperatures, and diseases.

name: INHA-U Korea
title: SA-Responsive Genetic Circuit Dual-Targeting Microbial Control SDual Biocontrol of Bradysia agrestis and Rhizosphere Fungi
abstract: Larvae of Bradysia agrestis damage crops and create wounds that facilitate infection by soilborne pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum. Backyard Guardian addresses both threats using Pseudomonas putida KT2440 engineered with a salicylic acid responsive NahR–XylS2 cascade regulating two defensive modules. We quantify SA in rhizosphere soil to determine whether naturally occurring concentrations fall within the circuit’s operating range and support reliable activation. We also evaluated designed Type VI secretion system to deliver the antifungal effector Tfe2 against F. oxysporum and Type I secretion system designed to export insecticidal proteins targeting B. agrestis larvae. Expanding the platform, we are engineering SA-responsive cascade for greater sensitivity to environmentally relevant SA concentrations and exchanging the T1SS toxin to assess modularity. By integrating environmental quantification, functional validation, and modular engineering, Backyard Guardian aims to establish a versatile microbial platform for targeted root protection while reducing reliance on conventional pesticides and supporting sustainable crop production.

name: Institut-Le-Rosey-CH
title: AURA
abstract:
AURA is developing an easy-to-use inline biosensor for early detection of subclinical mastitis in dairy cattle. Integrated into milking machines, it aims to support targeted treatment, reduce antibiotic use and veterinary costs, and improve animal welfare.

The sensor uses Field-Effect Transistor (FET) technology to detect bta-miR223, a milk microRNA associated with inflammation and subclinical mastitis. Its surface carries a DNA “catapult” designed to bind this target. Binding changes the DNA’s shape, altering the local electrical field and producing a measurable change in current. Reference electrodes help calibrate readings for differences between milk samples.

By monitoring each cow multiple times daily, AURA aims to identify infection before visible symptoms appear. The system is designed for straightforward integration into milking equipment, with minimal maintenance and technical expertise required.

name: Ionis-Paris
title: NEWT - Next-generation Enzymatic Waterborne-pathogen Treatment
abstract:
Driven by climate crisis, hydroponics is emerging as an alternative to soil farming, offering higher yield and resource efficiency. However, closed-loop systems remain vulnerable to waterborne pathogens. Pythium causes root rot, weakening or killing leafy greens and herbs. Countermeasures are energy-intensive and environmentally damaging, causing toxic runoff, disrupting root microbiota, and driving resistance.

NEWT (Next-generation Enzymatic Waterborne-pathogen Treatment) is a biocontrol agent detecting and treating infection in real time. We engineer Pseudomonas putida, a rhizobacterium mutualistic with plants, to release lytic enzymes only upon recognition of Pythium cell wall biomarkers via a Two-Component System with a Biomarker-Binding Module. Bacteria act against pathogens only when detected, while promoting plant growth. We assess the transformation of P. putida KT2440 and whether the enzyme can be expressed successfully while maintaining bioactivity. Replacing unsustainable countermeasures with an autonomous, bio-based solution, NEWT aims to protect roots and support sustainable agriculture.

name: MammothEdu-East
title: BioCall: Calling Nature Back to the City
abstract: A sticky bicycle seat, a car coated in sugary droplets, a pavement beneath a tree that never seems clean—these everyday nuisances can share one source: aphid honeydew. Managing aphids on urban street trees requires balancing pest control with the protection of surrounding ecosystems. BioCall combines synthetic biology and chemical ecology to explore a different approach: communicating through nature’s own chemical signals. Using engineered yeast, we develop biosynthetic modules for five volatile semiochemicals: (E)-β-farnesene, methyl salicylate, β-caryophyllene, linalool, and limonene. Through enzyme-source comparison, promoter tuning, and multigene assembly attempts, we work toward a modular platform for producing and combining these signals. Our goal is to influence aphid behavior and recruit natural enemies such as ladybirds, helping reduce honeydew pollution and pesticide dependence. BioCall envisions urban pest management that works with ecological relationships to make greener cities more livable.

name: Muenster-University
title: P.A.C. Immunity -Protect And Capture-
abstract: Plant diseases cause significant crop losses worldwide. To induce pathogen resistance, the current approach demands actively searching for natural occuring resistance genes in a wide range of organisms. Sadly, this approach is highly time-consuming and resource-intensive. Further, pathogens have shown a remarkable ability to adapt to newfound resistances, rendering them useless. Our project aims to transform plant immunity into a programmable system by engineering natural immune receptors, which recognize conserved pathogen proteases and trigger a direct and holistic defense response. Our projects goal is to develop an open-source modular platform that enables the rapid, precise design of tailored disease resistance for a wide range of crops. -We skip blindly searching for resistance, we design them.-

name: NACIS SHANGHAI
title: MelanoShield: Melanin-Protected Bt Cry1Ac for Sustainable Control of Lepidopteran Pests
abstract: The diamondback moth (Plutella xylostella), a major cruciferous pest, causes USD 4–5 billion in annual global losses. While Bt biopesticides are environmentally friendly alternatives to chemical pesticides, their broad use is constrained by unstable efficacy under UV irradiation and total field usage costs. To tackle these constraints, we developed MelanoShield, integrating UV shielding for Bt Cry1Ac and toxin-delivery engineering, together with two hardware prototypes to increase field application efficiency. Using E. coli W3110(DE3), we built a melanin–Cry1Ac co-production system yielding 1.80 g/L melanin with tyrosine feeding; 0.05 g/L melanin blocked 95.4% of UV light. We engineered an SmChiA–Cry1Ac fusion construct to facilitate toxin penetration through the insect peritrophic matrix via linker optimization (expression optimization ongoing). Separately, we designed an ESM-2 protein engineering workflow that identified MelA W144K, which increased the titer by 14.5% over wild type (from 0.55 ± 0.04 g/L to 0.63 ± 0.03 g/L).

name: NEFU-China
title: AAAgri——an AAA-grade（Accurate、Alternative、AI-assisted） pest control strategy via sustainable biomanufacturing
abstract:
AAAgri develops an AAA-grade pest control strategy via sustainable biomanufacturing, producing chrysanthemic acid in engineered Yarrowia lipolytica. Our approach centers on three "A" pillars:
 
Accurate: Green, relatively specific pyrethrins from chrysanthemic acid enable eco-friendly pest management, block vector-borne disease transmission, and serve as high-demand precursors for public health drugs.
Alternative: We upcycle low-value waste lipids as the sole carbon source, converting waste into high-value green pest control compounds.
AI-assisted: AI-assisted protein engineering optimizes rate-limiting enzymes in the MVA pathway, boosting pathway efficiency and chrysanthemic acid titers.
 
Long-term, we aim to establish a robust "waste-lipid-to-chrysanthemic-acid" platform for agriculture and public health, while developing a transferable high-DMAPP precursor module for universal isoprenoid biosynthesis.

name: NJTECH-CHINA-A
title: Engineering and Immobilization of NJF26: Exploring Its Application in Zearalenone (ZEN) Detoxification
abstract: Zearalenone (ZEN) contaminates maize, wheat and feed and causes reproductive and developmental toxicity in livestock. Conventional adsorption and chemical treatments lack selectivity and may damage nutrients. We built an integrated pipeline around the ZHD-family hydrolase NJF26: computational screening identified the enzyme, NJTECH-evolve and NJF-DuoStab prioritized mutants, expression optimization and site-directed mutagenesis produced improved variants, and calcium-alginate immobilization enabled reuse. NJF26 and the S33G/Y99V mutant degraded ZEN efficiently, and the immobilized beads retained activity over four uses, supporting a potential application in corn wet milling and feed detoxification.

name: NKU-China
title: Field Detective: A Yeast Biosensor for Plant-Parasitic Nematodes
abstract: Plant-parasitic nematodes damage crops underground; by the time growers notice the symptoms, it is often too late for effective intervention. NemaKlear aims to enable affordable risk screening using yeast engineered to convert nematode chemical signals into yellow betaxanthin. We confirmed expression and plasma-membrane localization of the fungal receptor GPR2 in yeast and constructed computationally selected variants, contributing basic parts for biosensor development. Molecular docking and dynamics guided receptor selection; signaling and dual-channel models explored target-density estimation amid background nematodes; economic modeling assessed when testing could improve treatment decisions. Surveys, expert interviews, and farm visits sharpened our focus on pre-planting screening and brought affordability, sampling quality, and soil interference into research discussions and test-strip development. By connecting receptor engineering, predictive modeling, and stakeholder feedback, NemaKlear lays the groundwork for accessible nematode detection and more informed crop protection.

name: OTIA-Hangzhou
title: Detect the Invisible
abstract: The moldiness of stored grains is a long-standing issue in food security: changes in temperature and humidity allow Aspergillus flavus to infect corn and peanuts, and produce aflatoxin B₁ before visible mold spots appear. Traditional detection methods such as high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) are accurate, but are limited by laboratory conditions, time-consuming and costly, resulting in the lack of practical early screening methods in grassroots warehouses. Therefore, we have developed a four-promoter whole-cell biosensor, in which hipB, dkgB, evgA and elfA drive the luxCDABE genome, converting Aspergillus flavus-related volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into bioluminescent signals that do not require exogenous substrates to self-illuminate. Chemically defined VOC mixtures can simulate the characteristic markers of different infection stages, and the combined interpretation of these four reporter genes can serve as early warning and later toxin indicators.

name: Oxford
title: NECTAR
abstract: NECTAR is a programmable RNAi biopesticide platform that integrates optimised strategies for the design, production, and delivery of dsRNA targeting Varroa mites. Combined with extensive in vivo testing, NECTAR has been developed as an accessible, easy-to-deploy therapeutic solution to a global threat to honeybee health.

name: Rochester
title: VERDANT (Vip3A Engineered Response for Defense Against Natural Threats)
abstract: Millions of tons of synthetic pesticides are applied to agricultural land annually across the world. Not only does the consistent use of synthetic pesticides contribute to environmental harm by damaging surrounding ecosystems, but these chemicals can also become less effective over time due to the evolution of resistance in pest populations. Our project aims to solve this issue by engineering a bacterial chassis to produce VIP3A, a natural pesticide, in response to methyl salicylate, a volatile organic compound that plants produce under pest-related stress. By producing a natural pesticide only when it is needed, we can reduce the amount of synthetic pesticides that are used on plants while slowing the development of insect resistance.

name: SHSD
title: BnDREB1C Overexpression in Arabidopsis: Toward Shorter-Season Rapeseed
abstract:
Rapeseed (Brassica napus) has a relatively long growth period, limiting its integration into crop rotation and multiple-cropping systems and the use of winter-fallow farmland. To explore a genetic approach to shortening this period, we overexpressed BnDREB1C, a rapeseed CBF/DREB1-family transcription factor, in Arabidopsis thaliana.
We constructed an overexpression vector and performed Agrobacterium-mediated floral dipping. Following antibiotic screening and molecular identification, RT-qPCR showed 4.4–11.9-fold higher relative BnDREB1C expression in five overexpression plants than in wild-type controls. These plants flowered earlier and matured sooner, suggesting that BnDREB1C can influence plant developmental timing.
Engagement with farmers, researchers, and other stakeholders helped us understand practical needs and challenges. Although further validation in rapeseed is needed, our results support BnDREB1C as a promising candidate for developing shorter-season rapeseed, with potential benefits for cropping flexibility and farmland utilization.

name: SHSID
title: PlantGuard: Based on a Synthetic Biology Dual-Module System for Coordinated Drought Management in Plants
abstract: To address global water scarcity and frequent droughts—where conventional irrigation relies on human experience and often leads to over- or delayed watering—we present  PlantGuard, a synthetic-biology-based dual-module drought management system using Saccharomyces cerevisiae as the chassis. The alert module drives expression of the blue chromoprotein amilCP under drought-inducible promoters, turning gel beads from white to blue upon water deficit as an intuitive visual warning. The soil-improvement module expresses dcsA and hasA-hasB to synthesize biodegradable cellulose and hyaluronic acid polymers in situ, enhancing rhizosphere water retention. Together, the two modules achieve "water retention + alerting." An accompanying ADRS hardware integrates in-situ sensing, ESP32 edge computing, wireless networking, and a mobile app to form a closed "sense–decide–respond" loop, offering a precise, autonomous, and sustainable water-management solution for both home gardening and large-scale agriculture.

name: Sorbonne University
title: PureGrain-Zen
abstract: PureGrain is a modular cell-free biosensing platform that turns molecular recognition into a nucleic-acid signal and a fluorescent read-out. Our proof of concept targets zearalenone, a mycotoxin found in cereals and feed. We combine an aptamer, a DNA trigger and a toehold switch, supported by structural modelling and the Apta2Switch-Studio design software. Interviews with experts, regulators and feed producers shaped our requirements. Experimental validation of the full ZEN-to-fluorescence pathway is still ongoing.

name: SRE-Shanghai
title: Fishfriend
abstract: Bacterial fish diseases are a major challenge to the sustainable development of aquaculture, causing significant economic losses worldwide. Conventional control strategies rely heavily on antibiotics, which contribute to antimicrobial resistance, environmental contamination, and drug residues in aquatic products. To address these issues, our project employs synthetic biology to engineer Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a microbial cell factory for the biosynthesis of 1,8-cineole, a naturally occurring monoterpene with broad-spectrum antibacterial activity. The produced 1,8-cineole is expected to inhibit or eliminate pathogenic bacteria responsible for bacterial fish diseases, providing an environmentally friendly alternative to conventional antibiotics. As a biodegradable natural compound with low toxicity to humans and minimal environmental impact, 1,8-cineole offers significant advantages in terms of biosafety and sustainability. By combining renewable microbial production with natural antimicrobial compounds, our approach aims to reduce antibiotic dependence while promoting healthier aquaculture practices.

name: SZ-SHD
title: S.A.F.E. Crops: Smart Anti-Freeze Endophytes for Crops
abstract: Unpredictable frost events remain a severe natural disaster that drastically limits agricultural crop yields. To address this vulnerability, we are engineering the Bacillus subtilis 168Δ4 strain to function as a frost-resilient endophyte capable of producing anti-freeze proteins or protective simple sugars. A low-temperature-responsive gene circuit will autonomously control the synthesis and release of these frost-resistance substances when the plant is exposed to freezing stress. We will establish this beneficial endophytic relationship by inoculating the plants through seed soaking or direct foliar spraying.

name: SZU-China
title: Ciricide: Multitarget cirRNA Pesticide Platform Integrating Circular RNA, with Minicell Based Production and Smart Release
abstract: Rapeseed, one of the world’s three major oil crops, suffers severe yield and quality losses caused by Sclerotinia stem rot. Team SZU-China develops an RNAi biopesticide built around innovatively structured dumbbellshaped cirRNA. We target three key virulence genes of S. sclerotiorum. With no free termini, this topologically stabilized cirRNA withstands nuclease digestion and achieves much higher environmental stability than linear dsRNA. Engineered E. coli minicells act as smart delivery carriers: they autonomously enrich and encapsulate cirRNA during biosynthesis, protect the payload from enzymatic degradation, and lyse to release cirRNA under the acidic microenvironment secreted by the pathogen. We also develop dedicated cirRNA intelligent design software and promote its industrial application. This reusable platform integrates computational design, molecular engineering, experimental validation and iterative optimization, providing the iGEM community with a reusable cirRNA toolkit and establishing a complete systematic workflow for developing multi-target cirRNA biopesticides.

name: TUS-Japan
title: Soilmate
abstract: Over one billion hectares of agricultural land worldwide are affected by soil salinization — a crisis driven by climate change, rising sea levels, and unsustainable irrigation practices. As arable land shrinks, ensuring stable food production for a growing global population becomes increasingly urgent. At the heart of this problem is salt-induced ethylene accumulation in plants, which stunts growth and devastates crop yields. Our team is engineering Bacillus subtilis to display ACC deaminase — an enzyme that degrades the ethylene precursor ACC — directly on its cell surface. Using a novel combination of the Twin-arginine translocation (Tat) secretion pathway and a LysM domain anchor, we aim to deliver a stable, active enzyme to the plant root environment without genetically modifying crops themselves. Our approach offers a scalable, plant-safe biological solution to one of agriculture's most pressing threats.

name: UPF-Barcelona
title: Vinesys
abstract: In 2024, Catalan reservoirs fell to 14.3% of capacity and vineyards could no longer count on the water they need. Vinesys engineers Bacillus subtilis to colonise the vine’s roots and overexpress γ-PGA, a biopolymer that retains water, and ACC deaminase, which degrades the precursor of the plant’s stress hormone ethylene. Since both molecules are counterproductive when there's no drought, their production must be conditional. We conceptualized a double authentication factor: an osmotic stress promoter and a salt-dependent intein inside the proteins of interest that splices only when intracellular K⁺ rises. Proteins become functional only when both agree. Our candidate intein HutMCM2 activates at 1.5 M salt, well above the 600-725 mM our chassis reaches, so we tried to lower its threshold in silico. This same approach is not limited to vineyards. Agriculture takes around 70% of the world’s freshwater and our design could be adapted to other crops.

name: URV-Tarragona
title: SCENTINEL: A Cell-Free OBP-Based Biosensor for Early Detection of Grapevine Fungal Infections
abstract: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe necator) threatens global viticulture, driving routine chemical treatments like copper and sulfur that severely contaminate soils. Early detection remains critical, as initial infections are visually undetectable.   SCENTINEL is a cell-free, non-GMO biosensing platform designed for early detection of defense-related plant volatile organic compounds (VOCs), primarily methyl salicylate (MeSA). Using our custom Python framework, SCENTINEL CODE, candidate Odorant-Binding Proteins (OBPs) were selected by scoring binding affinity, selectivity, and mixture discrimination. Optimized OBPs were expressed in Escherichia coli, purified via Strep-tag, and immobilized onto nanoporous anodic alumina (NAA) chips. Exposure to MeSA induced a measurable optical shift, providing solid proof of concept for volatile detection. Tailored for winegrower accessibility, SCENTINEL advances precision viticulture to significantly minimize preventative fungicide applications.

name: UW-Poland
title: HYPPE: a foundation model for fungal promoters and a toolkit designed to test it
abstract: Filamentous fungi produce antibiotics, enzymes and antifungal metabolites, yet remain almost unengineered: they transform at low efficiency, grow slowly, and have almost no characterised regulatory parts. For Trichoderma there is no measured promoter library and no model mapping promoter sequence to expression. HYPPE is a foundation model of fungal promoters trained from scratch on a corpus we assembled: 2,702 deposited RNA-seq runs requantified into 2,332 comparable samples across twenty genomes, every growth condition annotated by hand. It encodes a promoter as discrete hierarchical symbols rather than a dense vector, so sequences can be read, edited and decoded back to DNA, and reaches a rank correlation of 0.689 on a test split opened once. For the bench we measured a transformation protocol for T. atroviride, and built pHYPPE, which reports promoter strength as a ratio of two reporters, cancelling copy number and nuclear context.

name: VUB-Brussels
title: VUBzzz – AI-Guided Biocontrol of Vespa velutina Using A-ENA Nanofibers
abstract: The rapid spread of the Asian hornet (Vespa velutina) across Europe threatens native biodiversity and pollination-dependent agriculture. Existing control methods, such as manual trapping, have proven largely insufficient. VUBzzz proposes a targeted biocontrol strategy combining engineered nanofibers with computer vision-based species verification. Our approach centers on A-ENA nanofibers, derived from Bacillus thuringiensis and developed at our host lab (VIB-VUB Centre for Structural Biology), which naturally cluster spores and other biomolecules. We have functionalized these fibers to improve adhesion to insect cuticle, loading them with Beauveria bassiana spores as the active biocontrol agent. Because fiber-based targeting alone cannot achieve species-level specificity, we integrate a YOLO-based AI detection system into a custom box trap. The system confirms the presence of V. velutina before allowing entry into a secondary chamber where the hornet contacts the fiber-spore payload, maximizing specificity while minimizing non-target impact.

name: Worldshaper-Shanghai
title: SweetCycle: Enzyme Engineering of Steviol Glycosyltransferases for Enhanced Rebaudioside M Production
abstract: Reducing sugar without compromising taste demands better sweeteners. Rebaudioside M (Reb M) offers a clean, sucrose-like taste, but its low natural abundance and costly purification limit wider use. SweetCycle combines glycosyltransferase engineering with Stevia hairy-root screening to address this challenge. We constructed eight variants of SrUGT91D2 and SrUGT76G1 and evaluated them through tobacco transient expression followed by screening in Stevia rebaudiana hairy roots. In this preliminary screen, SrUGT76G1 T284I showed approximately 42% higher estimated Reb M content than wild type, identifying a promising candidate for further validation. Guided by stakeholder engagement and techno-economic modeling, we envision applying these candidates to enzymatic conversion and using hairy-root screening to support future crop improvement. Our work connects enzyme design with evaluation in the source plant, laying the groundwork for more accessible, better-tasting stevia ingredients.

name: Aix-Marseille
title: Antibio Wars
abstract:
Nowadays, antibiotics usage is increasing worldwide, and these end up in the environment. Indeed, multiple antibiotics are found in surface and underground waters. The presence of antibiotics in the environment increases the risk of a global bacterial antibiotic resistance threat. Sulfonamides are antibiotics well known to be disseminated in the environment when rejected after being used to treat humans or by the pharmaceutical industries.
We wants to address that problem by providing an enzyme-based solution. We Transformed Bl21 and C41 strain of E.coli to produce 5 different laccases.
Laccases are oxydases that catalyze the oxidation of phenolic compounds. It has been proved that several laccases have the capacity to degrade sulfonamides. 
We purified these laccases, characterized and attached them on a surface, first via a 6His-tag and then via a cellulose binding module to test their ability to act as a filter able to degrade sulfonamides

name: Beijing-HS
title: A Uric Acid Degradation Scheme for Aquaculture Wastewater Based on Synthetic Biology
abstract: Uric acid is a typical high-risk nitrogenous pollutant in livestock and aquaculture wastewater. When discharged into water bodies, it can easily cause environmental problems such as water acidification and eutrophication. Current traditional physical, chemical, and single-microorganism degradation methods suffer from limitations including low efficiency, incomplete substrate coverage, and a tendency to cause secondary pollution. This project aims to construct a dual-functional cascade system for both uric acid detection and degradation, converting uric acid in poultry manure wastewater into allantoin. Directly used for crop irrigation, the harmful effects on crop root growth are mitigated, as allantoin actually benefits plant growth. When discharged into water bodies, this approach avoids causing water acidification and eutrophication. The engineered bacteria will ultimately be prepared into sodium alginate-immobilized beads suitable for fluidized bed reactors, providing a green, non-polluting, low-cost, and recyclable remediation solution for the bioremediation of contaminated water from aquaculture.

name: Benenden
title: AQUA SHIELD
abstract:
Heavy metal contamination poses a severe public health threat, but current detection methods fall short. Laboratory instruments are accurate but slow and expensive, while portable chemical kits cannot distinguish between specific metals, leading to false positives, a flaw our team experienced firsthand.

To address this, we engineered AQUA SHIELD: two specific, whole-cell bacterial biosensors in E. coli TOP10. Our mercury biosensor uses the MerR–PmerT circuit with GFP. To guide future optimization, we employed ESM-2 AI models to computationally screen over 2,700 protein substitutions and prioritize MerR mutants for enhanced sensitivity. Our lead biosensor is a novel composite part using the PbrR–PpbrA system to control mCherry. Experimental results validated both baseline systems, demonstrating strong, target-specific fluorescence with no cross-reactivity to other metals.

Paired with a custom 3D-printed drone for safe, remote water sampling, our platform transforms heavy metal detection into an accessible, field-deployable tool.

name: Berlin
title: Sense PFASt - Yeast-Based Biosensor for PFAS Detection
abstract: ‘Forever chemicals’ are everywhere. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are toxic, persistent, and pervasive chemicals that accumulate silently in ecosystems and the human body. In response, the European Union is aggressively tightening regulations on permissible PFAS levels in drinking water, forcing industries to find immediate solutions. However, standard quantitative methods are too costly and slow for routine adoption. To overcome this limitation, we are developing a yeast-based biosensor to screen for PFAS in less than an hour and at a fraction of the cost. Rather than relying on a single mechanism, our architecture integrates three distinct strategies: a synthetic transcriptional reporter, a binding-induced conformational sensor, and an inducible bacterial promoter layer for amplified signal detection. This parallel profiling builds a comprehensive library to optimize the sensor’s sensitivity and specificity without compromising the response time. Ultimately, expanding this framework links on-site detection with tailored enzymatic degradation for complete aquatic remediation.

name: BYHS-CHN
title: BioShield: Biology for Controlled Surface Treatment
abstract: BioShield explores how synthetic biology could support controlled surface treatment of asbestos-relevant materials. We studied three complementary modules: oxalic-acid production, metal-responsive circuits, and a candidate MgFP/VsTyr protein material. In a seven-condition copper reporter comparison, the ZupT-containing PFL design produced higher output than the NR design, alongside higher baseline expression. Separate assays examined metal readouts, oxalic-acid signals and recovered magnesium-silicate solids. Protein-material observations guided a revision of the MgFP construct. Clinicians, researchers, construction professionals and communities helped frame research priorities around exposure prevention, containment and responsible material management. Our education work combined completed classroom dialogue, visual storytelling and a documented bilingual game prototype for future testing. We share construct references, measurement calculations and experimental lessons for future teams. These component-level and proxy-material studies establish a basis for further testing; integrated treatment performance and asbestos-specific risk reduction remain to be demonstrated.

name: DTU-Denmark
title: ByeByeBlade: A SynBio approach to Wind Turbine Blade Waste
abstract: Current end-of-life wind turbine blade treatment routes often recycle the mineral fraction but not  organic products from the resin. ByeByeBlade investigated the enzymatic degradation of thermoset resin to explore an alternative valorisation route. We identified relevant laccases and unspecific peroxygenases (UPO). Developed a drylab pipeline to identify homologs and design mutants with truncations, wider channels and higher solvent tolerances. We worked with 37 enzymes in Escherichia coli and Komagataella phaffii, including literature enzymes, previously unexpressed homologs, and our own designs. Four purified laccases and three UPOs showed activity on our substrate N,N-Bis(2-hydroxypropyl)-p-toluidine, a model compound of an epoxy thermoset resin. MALDI-TOF suggests substrate depletion and new product formation. On an extract from cured epoxy resin, active ItL-03 removed a peak that persisted in all controls. Results for other homologs and mutants remain inconclusive. We also conducted a life cycle assessment of the process.

name: GeorgetownPrep
title: SENTINEL-LOOP: Detecting, Removing, and Verifying Lead and Cadmium in Water
abstract: Finding lead or cadmium in water is only the first step; a practical system should also remove the metals and confirm that treatment worked. SENTINEL-LOOP connects these tasks in one modular framework. We designed two engineered whole-cell biosensors: CadR/PcadA-lacZ for cadmium and PbrR/PpbrA-amilCP for lead. We paired them with a removal module displaying the metal-binding domains PbBD and EC20 on bacterial surfaces. For independent verification, we developed a bismuth-film screen-printed-electrode workflow using square-wave anodic stripping voltammetry to measure remaining Cd(II) and Pb(II). We also built mechanistic models and an open-source analysis pipeline for sensor response, adsorption, column breakthrough, and electrochemical peak analysis, with provenance labels separating simulations from experimental evidence. Full wet-lab and electrochemical validation was not completed before the Wiki Freeze; we plan to complete the remaining experiments before our judging session. The completed work provides a transparent, modular foundation for a self-verifying water-treatment system.

name: Harvard
title: MlrAcle on the Charles
abstract: Algal blooms in the Charles River are a significant environmental and public health issue within the Greater Boston area. Overgrowth of cyanobacteria can lead to the production and release of algal toxins such as microcystins which can cause liver damage in humans. We aim to reduce microcystin levels by engineering bacteria to produce encapsulins, self-assembling protein components designed to carry a bacterial enzyme called MlrA to degrade microcystins. By linking encapsulin production to the detection of cyanobacterial overgrowth, this system is intended to eliminate microcystins specifically during bloom conditions, providing a targeted strategy to reduce toxin levels and improve the safety of the Charles River for surrounding communities and ecosystems

name: HK League
title: Bioprinted ElectroMining: Engineering Microbes and Hydrogel Devices for Battery Metal Recovery
abstract: Electric vehicle growth is increasing the need to recover nickel, cobalt and lithium from spent batteries. Bioprinted ElectroMining explores a biological recovery stage intended to complement upstream recycling. We designed six candidate metal-binding proteins and twelve plasmid constructs, immobilised construct-bearing Escherichia coli in calcium alginate, and performed preliminary metal assays. A modular six-stage bead cartridge was operated with laboratory-prepared mixed-metal solution through loading, washing and separate elution of cartridge pairs. In parallel, we developed a syringe-based bioprinter and BioPrintCAD to explore printed hydrogel geometries for future cartridge designs. This laboratory proof-of-concept study connects protein design, cell immobilisation, measurement and device engineering. The operated bead cartridge and proposed bioprinted cartridge are distinct development stages. Further work will test protein-specific capture, selective separation, product purity, reuse and performance with real battery leachate. Our goal is to establish a practical research platform for evaluating biological approaches to battery-metal recovery.

name: HK-PLKNPLC
title: Engineered Lanmodulin Variants for Selective Recovery of Terbium from Fluorescent Lamp E-Waste Leachate
abstract: Terbium (Tb³⁺) is concentrated at 3.4 wt% in fluorescent lamp phosphor powder yet less than 1% is currently recovered, because dissolved phosphor leachate contains large molar excesses of yttrium (Y³⁺), lanthanum (La³⁺), europium (Eu³⁺), and cerium (Ce³⁺) alongside major non-REE impurities, and no low-cost selective capture platform exists. This project engineers lanmodulin (LanM) from Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 to selectively capture Tb³⁺ from this matrix. Three variants — T90Y, E95D, and D43N — are designed to shift LanM's EF-hand coordination geometry toward the smaller Tb³⁺ ionic radius (9-coordinate: 1.095 Å), based on crystallographic distances measured directly from the 1.01 Å X-ray structure PDB 8FNS. All constructs are expressed as His₆-LanM-GS-CBDcex fusions in E. coli NiCo21(DE3) and immobilised on microcrystalline cellulose. T90Y introduces a Tyr antenna providing built-in Tb³⁺ luminescence at 545 nm without additional reagents. Wild-type LanM serves as a benchmark.

name: HS-Kentucky
title: A Dual Approach to PFAS Detection: Transcriptomic and Cell-Free Biosensors for Environmental Monitoring
abstract: PFAS are persistent “forever chemicals” that contaminate water and soil and pose health risks. Current detection methods are costly and inaccessible, so we aim to engineer a low-cost biosensor with a visible fluorescent signal. We pursued two approaches. In the cell-based approach, we exposed E. coli BL21(DE3) to two PFOA concentrations at three time points and profiled transcriptome-wide changes. Genes including glpA, gadE, cadA, and cadB were significantly up-regulated across all six conditions, making them promoter candidates. In the cell-free approach, we mutated the maltose-binding protein to enhance FRET signals and PFAS specificity. Using LigandMPNN, AlphaFold3, Gromacs, and OpenMM, they generated and validated over 50 mutant structures. A final mutant increased docking scores by 2.7 to 3.4 kcal/mol and was analyzed with FPMOD to simulate a FRET sensor environment. The results provide promoter shortlists for cloning and validation, plus protein targets, advancing a field-deployable PFOA biosensor for testing.

name: HUBU-WUHAN
title: Engineering a Two-Strain System for Naphthalene Degradation and Salicylic Acid-Based Biosensing
abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are widespread, persistent pollutants; global emissions of 16 priority PAHs reached higher recent years. Naphthalene, a frequently detected PAH in urban soils and its Group 2B IARC classified. Conventional detection is costly and laboratory-bound. We developed a two-strain E. coli system: a degrader strain carrying the nah cluster from Pseudomonas putida G7 converts naphthalene to salicylic acid, which a sensor strain detects via a bidirectional NahR–Psal/Pr-driven eGFP reporter, i.e. NahR-salicylic acid complex activates Psal-driven eGFP. Through multi-layer engineering—promoter optimization (100 to 20 μM), NahR saturation mutagenesis (20 to 0.2 μM), and ARTP evolution (0.2 to 0.05 μM), achieved lowest detection limit of 0.05 μM, the lowest reported to date. Promoter replacement, and Fe²⁺ tuning lead to near-complete naphthalene degradation within 4 h at low concentrations (20–100 μM). Integrated portable device with mobile App, enables on-site PAH screening, leading to future field deployment.

name: IISER-TVM
title: SANJEEVANI
abstract:
India’s mines leave behind tailings, the waste left once ore is processed. Heavy metals seep from these dumps into soil and groundwater, surfacing years later as chronic illness in nearby villages, most of them tribal. Today such land is dug out and dumped elsewhere, washed with acid, or capped over. These traditional Bioremeditation methods are slow, costly.

Sanjeevani is a living alternative. We are engineering the moss Physcomitrium patens to pull these metals into its tissue. We would spray it onto contaminated rock and tailings by hydroseeding, then harvest it with the metals still inside.

The moss is mostly haploid and recombines readily, so edits land where we put them and show at once. We are strengthening how much metal it takes up and how much it can safely hold, to further improve this bio-engineered design to tackle this problem in an environment friendly way

name: KCIS
title: ReBile: Reprogramming Waste Bile Acids into Therapeutic UDCA
abstract: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is an important therapeutic agent widely used for the treatment of liver and biliary diseases and remains the only FDA-approved drug for primary biliary cholangitis. However, current production methods face significant challenges, including low efficiency, complex chemical synthesis, and ethical concerns associated with traditional bear bile extraction. To address these limitations, we developed a sustainable biosynthesis platform that converts poultry bile waste into high-value UDCA. Using Escherichia coli as a microbial chassis, we engineered a biocatalytic pathway by introducing and optimizing 7α- and 7β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, while enhancing cofactor regeneration to improve conversion efficiency. Computational protein engineering was further applied to optimize key enzymes and maximize production performance. By transforming agricultural by-products into valuable pharmaceuticals, our project combines synthetic biology, enzyme engineering, and circular bioeconomy principles to enable greener UDCA production and promote sustainable waste utilization.

name: Keystone
title: Cracking the Code of Coffee Wastewater — Engineered Microflora "Dismantle" Organic Pollution
abstract: Yunnan is China's primary coffee-producing region. However, the direct discharge of untreated coffee wastewater from small-scale processing facilities has led to severe water pollution and ecological damage. Conventional treatment methods are limited by high costs, high energy consumption, and low removal efficiency, which hinder their practical application. To address these challenges, this project adopts a synthetic biology approach to construct two engineered yeast strains with a coordinated division of labor, each designed to target and degrade specific components of coffee wastewater—pectin and lactic acid, respectively. These strains will be co-immobilized using a sodium alginate-chitosan matrix to achieve efficient and stable degradation performance. Additionally, a kill switch will be introduced to ensure biosafety by preventing environmental release. Collectively, this work aims to provide a safe, efficient, and low-cost synthetic biology-based solution for the treatment of high-strength acidic organic wastewater, offering significant scientific value for ecological protection.

name: LYON
title: BioThetis- binding TFA, the smallest forever chemical: protein design for cleaner water, shaped by society
abstract: PFAS, known as “forever chemicals”, persist in the environment and accumulate in water, soil and living organisms. Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), the smallest PFAS, is found in tap water across Europe and is difficult to remove with usual treatments. BioThetis proposes to capture TFA with protein binders anchored on cellulose and to release it by heating, with the aim of reusing the material. This year we designed and produced binders, from a natural enzyme scaffold and from de novo design, showed that they interact with TFA, and built cellulose-anchored versions. We also explored enzymatic degradation. The scaffold defluorinated difluoroacetate (DFA), a related compound, but not TFA, which led us to focus on capture. The project was shaped from the start by researchers, water professionals, associations, elected officials and the public, and we shared it through games, a short film, a video game, and school and public events.

name: Macquarie-Australia
title: MagniMO: Engineering Magnetic Microbes for 1,4-Dioxane Bioremediation and Recoverable Synthetic Biology Solutions
abstract:
MagniMO aims to address the persistent environmental challenge of 1,4-dioxane contamination in groundwater and wastewater through an innovative synthetic biology approach. 1,4-Dioxane is highly water-soluble, resistant to conventional treatment, and a potential human carcinogen. 

Our project investigates the use of a soluble di-iron monooxygenase (SDIMO) to support 1,4-dioxane degradation, alongside magnetite biomineralisation to enable magnetic cell recovery. By combining bioremediation with magnetic recovery, MagniMO explores a potential pathway towards more efficient and sustainable water treatment, with biocontainment and environmental safety central to future implementation. 

Beyond the laboratory, human practices shaped MagniMO through expert consultation, stakeholder engagement, and engineering design reviews. These practices guided the development of a safe and practical treatment approach. Our education and outreach programmes engaged diverse audiences through interactive workshops, school activities, university presentations, and community events. These initiatives made synthetic biology accessible while highlighting its potential to address environmental challenges and protect water resources.

name: Madrid-UCM
title: Encapsulated engineered microorganisms for phosphorus removal and revalorisation from wastewater
abstract: Phosphorus pollution from industrial wastewater is a major contributor to eutrophication, causing algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and damage to aquatic ecosystems. At the same time, phosphorus is a finite and strategically important resource. Our project, rePhlow aims to recover this phosphorus using biodegradable alginate capsules that combine microorganisms and enzymes to capture and process phosphorus from wastewater. These capsules would be used in a modular bioreactor to treat wastewater safely, prevent the release of engineered organisms, and allow the recovered phosphorus to be transformed into useful high-value products. By turning a pollutant into a resource, rePhlow connects wastewater treatment with circular economy principles.

name: MCA-SWIS
title: Pesticide Cleanup: Broad-Spectrum Degradation and Real-Time Monitoring of Organophosphate Pesticides
abstract:
Widespread use of organophosphorus pesticides, glyphosate and other agrochemicals in modern agriculture creates severe co contamination in soil and water, endangering ecological health and food safety. Conventional remediation techniques are hampered by high expenses and the risk of secondary pollution. With synthetic biology approaches, we built engineered Escherichia coli strains for colorimetric detection and substrate biotransformation, aiming project provides a low cost, efficient and sustainable bioremediation alternative.
We selected Escherichia coli DH5α as the cloning host and Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) as the expression host, and completed the construction of recombinant plasmids. For the sensing module, we constructed pETDuet-1-chpR-eforRed and pETDuet-1-phnF-AmilCP. For the biotransformation module, we constructed pET28a-OPD and pET28a-pelB-gat.

name: Missouri-Rolla
title: Metlock: A Modular, Reproducible Biomining Platform
abstract:
Growing demand for critical minerals has increased the need for sustainable metal recovery technologies. Metlock develops a modular synthetic biology platform using engineered *Escherichia coli* to investigate controlled zinc uptake, capture, and retention.

The platform integrates three interconnected modules: ZnuABC-mediated zinc uptake, AHL–LuxR-regulated gene expression, and an Ag43–SmtA fusion protein designed for zinc binding and surface display. Together, these modules aim to establish a tunable and reproducible system for biological metal recovery.

Experimental work demonstrated AHL-responsive fluorescence using a dual-plasmid LuxR/pLuxR-sfGFP reporter system. Subsequent engineering cycles focused on characterizing gene expression, refining experimental methods, and improving zinc uptake strategies. Parallel protein modeling efforts supported the development and optimization of the surface-display construct.

By combining genetic engineering, experimental characterization, and iterative design, Metlock aims to establish a versatile biomining platform that can be adapted for the recovery of zinc and other valuable metals.

name: MPAYF-USA
title: Environd ：Detection and remediation of 2,4-DNT
abstract:
2,4-Dinitrotoluene (2,4-DNT) is an important pollutant in the polyurethane foam industry chain and is characterized by high toxicity, carcinogenicity, and environmental persistence.
This project employs synthetic biology to construct an engineered microbial system that integrates “pollutant detection–signal response–pollutant degradation.” A YhaJ–PyqjF biosensor is utilized to enable rapid detection of 2,4-DNT, while the degradation pathway is reconstructed to achieve its efficient mineralization.
This system combines real-time monitoring, green remediation, and low cost advantages, providing an innovative solution for pollution control around furniture manufacturing and polyurethane material production industries.

name: NTHU Taiwan
title: CatharSys: Engineered Bacillus subtilis for TMAH Treatment in MBBR
abstract:
Tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) is a highly toxic chemical used in semiconductor photolithography. Its use in Hsinchu, a major semiconductor hub in Taiwan, highlights the need for safer wastewater treatment. Conventional biological treatment takes weeks or months to prepare microbial communities and consumes large amounts of electricity for aeration. It also produces excess sludge that requires further treatment. 
To address these problems, CatharSys introduces seven genes (Msil_3603–3609) from Methylocella silvestris BL2 into industrial Bacillus subtilis to enable the degradation of trimethylamine (TMA). We also promote biofilm growth on moving bed biofilm reactor (MBBR) carriers to improve bacterial retention. In addition, we developed CathaBench, a three-tank laboratory reactor with automated sensing and control, to test our system. Together with three layers of biosafety measures, CatharSys aims to reduce energy use and sludge production and support more sustainable semiconductor wastewater treatment.

name: NWU-CHINA
title: HYDRA: Engineering a Modular Aspergillus niger Platform for Complex Wastewater Remediation
abstract: Water pollution often involves mixtures of nutrients, heavy metals, and persistent organic contaminants, sometimes under saline conditions. Northwestern China illustrates this challenge: it contains headwaters of major river systems and extensive mining activity. Motivated by this regional context, we developed HYDRA, a modular wastewater remediation platform based on Aspergillus niger. At its core, we engineered seven specialized fungal strains, each designed to target a different organic pollutant or pollutant class. This division of labor is intended to enable flexible treatment configurations. Representative assays using real wastewater demonstrated 31.5% benzene removal and 44.9% styrene removal by engineered strains. The fungal chassis also tolerated 5% NaCl and achieved 63.3% phosphate removal and 57.2% Cd removal in separate assays. These findings lay a foundation for a configurable fungal consortium. HYDRA connects local water challenges with adaptable bioremediation, while future work will assess strain compatibility, pollutant fate, and long-term treatment performance.

name: NYU-Abu-Dhabi
title: DuneLock: Sand Stabilization through Gene Overexpression and Transgenesis
abstract: Sandy deserts, such as the Arabian Desert, are historically, culturally, and economically significant. However, for cities rising around them, sandy deserts are a hub for loose sediments that are continuously being re-suspended by winds, which then travel short and far distances, degrading air quality, decreasing visibility, coating solar panels, and jeopardizing daily life - with 800 million people affected globally. Dunelock focuses on sand stabilization by engineering a microbially-produced adhesive material. Gene overexpression of γ-PGA is used to enhance the stickiness of biofilms while exogenous gene expression of Carbonic Anhydrase is used to precipitate stabilizing crystals between sand grains, all whilst sequestering carbon dioxide and avoiding toxic gas release. With clearer air, Dunelock is a step towards a healthier outdoors.

name: NYU-New-York
title: PeBet: Plastic Degradation via Bacteria Consortium
abstract: Our project aims to solve the escalating issue of plastic pollution. As of currently, the amount of plastic that pollutes cities, oceans, and environments is exponential but the efforts put into reducing the amount of plastic on our earth is minimal. Current conventional means of recycling and degrading plastic are inefficient as they take years for only a small percentage of the plastic to be degraded. Our goal is to degrade the most common type of plastic, PET. In naturally occurring I. Sakainesis bacteria, there exists enzymes, PETase and MHETase, that degrade PET thoroughly and much more efficiently than conventional ways (mechanical and chemical). By creating an optimal environment via a tabletop bioreactor, we can control the conditions where our I. Sakainesis can degrade PET at its optimal rate.

name: Oakridge-HYD
title: BioChronos: A DNA-Based Environmental Memory System in E. coli
abstract: Transient contamination can escape periodic sampling. BioChronos explores a DNA-based exposure recorder in Escherichia coli through a copper-responsive sfGFP sensor (M1) and separate arabinose-controlled Bxb1 inversion modules. Four linked computational models guided architecture choices; simulation checks and an independent implementation assessed numerical robustness. Our preliminary M1 assay used three independently picked DH5alpha colonies: raw fluorescence at nominal 1000 micromolar copper was approximately 2.08-fold the zero-copper condition, while 1–200 micromolar showed no clear increase. This mismatch prompted model revision. Clone sequences remain unverified, controls are incomplete, and neither the memory modules nor the integrated recorder is experimentally validated. Stakeholder engagement informed proposed containment, retrieval and communication requirements. Our distributed high-school team addressed financial and geographical participation barriers while documenting unresolved inequities. We release Registry designs, reproducible models and experimental records to support future teams and scrutiny of both our findings and limitations.

name: RUM-UPRM
title: R-DetoX 2.5: Engineering Escherichia coli for RDX Bioremediation within a Serial Bioreactor System
abstract: RDX contamination threatens the environment and motivates the development of biological remediation strategies. R-DetoX 2.5 engineers Escherichia coli with the XplA/XplB enzyme system to target RDX, incorporating inducible and riboswitch-regulated genetic devices. In batch assays monitored by HPLC, the IPTG-inducible construct reduced extracellular RDX concentration by 85% within 20 hours, while abiotic controls remained unchanged. To translate this biological approach into a treatment process, we designed SeBiS 2.0, a proposed serial bioreactor system integrating bacterial growth, continuous treatment, biomass recirculation, and byproduct mitigation. Expert consultations informed process design and safety considerations, while educational activities engaged students and communities with synthetic biology and environmental remediation. By connecting biological engineering, process design, education, and stakeholder perspectives, R-DetoX 2.5 advances a research foundation for contained RDX bioremediation, with further validation needed to establish degradation pathways and treatment performance.

name: Saarland
title: OWLET: On Board Water Logger For Environmental Tracking
abstract: Industrial pollutants such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and cadmium enter rivers like the Saar, reducing water quality. Monitoring relies on a few fixed stations and lab analyses that take days. OWLET brings biosensing to the water. It is a hybrid platform that combines encapsulated whole-cell biosensors and a field hardware design for continuous biosensing, mapping and tracking of water pollutants.  The biosensors detect PAHs and heavy metals like cadmium. To read them in the field, we built a low-cost, 3D-printed fluorescence reader that pumps water into a six-well strip, measures fluorescence and converts it into fluorescein-equivalent units, validated with fluorescein standards and GFP-expressing E. coli. The reader is designed to ride on our boat, which samples, steers toward rising signals and tags each reading with its position, while a live dashboard shows the readings and the track. OWLET is a monitoring system that identifies hotspots for in-depth lab analysis.

name: SCAU-China
title: CyanoGuard
abstract: Microcystin-LR threatens freshwater safety during cyanobacterial blooms. CyanoGuard investigates an integrated approach to toxin monitoring and remediation using engineered bacteria, computational models and modular devices. We constructed START (Synthetic Trans-Acting Riboswitch with Triggering RNA) RNA-sensing circuits with LuxI/LuxR amplification and sfGFP/TurboRFP readout, compared circuit variants, and tested light-dependent growth control in a DAP-auxotrophic chassis. Structure-guided Trigger design and a focused RNA library support sensor development. A model using the previous seven days of environmental observations estimates total-microcystin exceedance risk; fluorescence calibration and literature-based degradation modelling support concentration mapping and treatment design. Our monitoring boat and detachable drone release module have documented prototype tests, design files and controller software. Stakeholder input shaped the project's screening role and need for laboratory confirmation, while outreach addressed toxin risks and protective actions. We share parts, methods and reusable resources to support further development.

name: SMS-Shenzhen
title: kisMET: A Biosorption Platform for Low-Concentration Metal Recovery from End-of-Pipe Battery Wastewater
abstract: Lithium-ion battery recycling retains low-concentration residual metal ions in end-of-pipe wastewater, causing resource loss and environmental burden with conventional chemical treatment. We present kisMET, a biosorption platform built on engineered Komagataeibacter rhaeticus that produces bacterial cellulose microspheres displaying metal-binding peptides to selectively capture Li⁺, Co²⁺, Ni²⁺ and Mn²⁺. Our chassis secretes cellulose and functional peptides synchronously in fermentation, forming reusable adsorbent microspheres. Through multi-stakeholder interviews with battery enterprises, regulatory experts and iGEM peers, we iteratively defined kisMET as a supplementary end-of-pipe treatment unit rather than a full replacement for existing processes. We performed TEA and LCA analysis to evaluate cost and carbon footprint, alongside public science outreach. This modular system provides a mild, low-reagent route for metal ion circularity, aligning with multiple UN SDGs, though scale-up and real wastewater validation remain ongoing.

name: Squirrel-Beijing
title: pNProbe: A Whole-Cell Biosensor for Bioavailable p-Nitrophenol Monitoring in Soil
abstract: p - Nitrophenol (pNP), a hazardous pollutant from pesticide, industrial and chemical processes, is common in agricultural soils, posing ecological and health risks. Conventional methods can't well reflect its bioavailable fraction. We developed pNProbe, a whole - cell biosensor. It screens and optimizes pNP - responsive elements, using fluorescent and chromoprotein reporters to convert pNP exposure into interpretable outputs. This enables easy, in - situ monitoring in various soils. pNProbe offers an accessible tool for soil pollution assessment, showing synthetic biology's role in sustainable agriculture.

name: Stockholm
title: T.I.D.E - Targeted Interception and Degradation of Endocrine disruptors
abstract:
Bisphenol A and its alternatives (BPA+) are widely used monomers in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins. BPA+ are endocrine-disrupting chemicals, they interfere with hormone-mediated pathways. Culminating in widespread dysregulation of reproductive, metabolic, and developmental processes, and in growth and developmental defects. Their ubiquitous presence has significant health risks to humans and aquatic animals, posing an environmental threat to population stability that is under researched and poorly understood. 

Our project, TIDE, is a modular 3-vector platform that integrates sensing, reporting, and bioremediation for BPA+. These modules permit specific targeting with broad-spectrum degradation. In parallel, we worked to redesign a receptor with BPA-alternative specificity. Due to the poorly understood risks of BPA alternatives, our team worked to educate and engage the public through multiple initiatives and to integrate the outcomes into our project design. These initiatives raised awareness of bisphenol risks and sustainable development, the role biotechnology could play in both.

name: THIS-China
title: ArtemiSilence: MSN-Mediated RNAi Delivery to Reduce Mugwort Pollen Allergens
abstract: Mugwort (Artemisia) pollen is a major trigger of fall seasonal allergies in Beijing and many other regions. Current control methods, such as large-scale plant removal and herbicide application, are non-specific and may damage urban ecosystems. ArtemiSilence aims to develop a plant-targeted strategy using mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) as carriers to deliver RNA interference (RNAi) molecules into mugwort plants. The delivered RNAi is designed to silence selected genes associated with pollen-allergen expression, thereby reducing allergen levels during flowering without eliminating the plants. We will identify candidate allergen-related genes, design RNAi molecules, optimize RNAi loading into MSNs and delivery to plant tissues, quantify gene-silencing efficiency and changes in allergen levels, and evaluate specificity, persistence, biosafety, and environmental feasibility. Our goal is to develop a precise and environmentally responsible approach to reducing exposure to airborne mugwort pollen allergens.

name: TJI-Seoul
title: CPS Cycle: Integrating Citrus Waste, Protein (Laccase(CotA)), and Soil for Post-Fire Restoration
abstract: Wildfires can leave soils chemically and biologically impaired, while citrus-processing waste remains an underused biomass resource. We developed the CPS Cycle, a synthetic biology platform combining processed citrus waste, recombinant CotA laccase, and soil for post-fire restoration research. CotA from Bacillus subtilis was expressed in Escherichia coli, optimized for soluble production, and validated using ABTS and guaiacol activity assays. Citrus waste was washed, dried, pulverized, and incorporated into soil to improve plant compatibility. The optimized CotA preparation was then integrated with processed citrus soil to create the final CPS material. In a simplified burned-biomass model, CotA treatment reduced detectable phenolic signal, while lettuce assays showed improved growth performance under selected CPS conditions.
