CotA-associated activity also remained detectable after incorporation into the citrus-soil matrix. Our work establishes a proof-of-concept for a non-living, recombinant-protein-based approach linking waste valorization, enzyme biotechnology, and environmental restoration.

name: TJUSLS-China
title: PUReCycle——Discovery and Engineering of PURases
abstract:
Polyurethane waste creates serious plastic-pollution challenges. MDI-based polyether polyurethane, occupying ~75% foam-market share, is hard to degrade naturally, and effective urethanases for its biorecycling are limited.
Following the DBTL cycle, our project integrated metagenomic mining and semi-rational enzyme engineering. From ~30 million metagenomic sequences in SoilMicrobeDB, GTDB and JGI, we performed multi-layer computational screening and selected 19 PUC urethanase candidates for wet-lab tests. We also engineered seed enzyme AbPURase through docking, MD simulation and site-directed mutagenesis. The double-point mutant AbPURase_DM2 exhibited high activity at both 50 °C and 60 °C. Using MDC as model substrate, we built a standardized UPLC activity-quantification system. This study enriches urethanase resources and supports future biological recycling of PU waste.

name: Toronto
title: PetaBite: Mapping Earth's Biodiversity to Discover Room-Temperature Plastic-Degrading Enzymes
abstract:
Plastic has become so abundant that its carbon content now exceeds that of all animals on Earth. Fortunately, nature offers an ecological solution with PETases, enzymes capable of degrading polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Previously, fewer than 500 validated sequences had been characterized, limiting humanity’s ability to discover variants suitable for industrial deployment. 

In response, we created the PETadex, the largest open-source database of plastic-degrading enzymes, by searching 27.3 million public sequencing datasets. This expanded the catalogue from 495 sequences to over 300 million naturally occurring homologs, unlocking unprecedented scale and diversity.

PetaBite creates an integrated workflow to leverage the database. We rank candidates with a protein language model trained on the PETadex, screen them with a high-throughput copper-release assay in E. coli, and further test them in our low-cost open-source bioreactors. Our goal: to discover and validate room-temperature PETases that surpass current benchmarks and enable scalable microplastic degradation.

name: UCL
title: SHELLter: A purification system valorising shellfish waste to filter platinum-based chemotherapy residues in hospital wastewater
abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy drugs such as cisplatin are life-saving, but their environmental impact has received far less attention than their clinical importance. Up to 90% of these cytotoxic drugs are excreted by chemotherapy patients unmetabolised, with 59% of this load persisting in surface water discharge. Meanwhile, around 2 million of the 16.9 million tonnes of seafood waste landfilled each year is chitin-rich shellfish waste, an abundant and underused resource. SHELLter links these two problems with a single solution. Our team proposes a sustainable enzymatic strategy to convert chitin from shellfish waste into chito-oligosaccharides, a heavy metal chelating agent. Using recombinantly produced novel enzymes such as a ChitinaseA-Chitin Deacetylase fusion, these chito-oligosaccharides are produced and incorporated into an adsorption cartridge for toilets, enabling cisplatin capture at the point of excretion. Ultimately, this system can transform into a platform technology, offering a sustainable bioremediation strategy to tackle heavy metal water contamination.

name: UMaryland
title: AEGIS (Aquatic E. coli Guard and Interception using Sinorhizobium)
abstract: In specific areas, the E. coli spikes are much higher due to combined sewer systems. These systems, unlike the standard sewer system, have connected storm water and sewage pipes, which can lead to an overflow of combined sewage and storm water beyond the flow regulator and into the local waterways. Inspired by the recent Potomac River sewage overflow in Maryland, AEGIS addresses the local issue of combined sewage systems, which often overflow into streams, by killing diarrheagenic E. coli in water contaminated by sewage. This will help countless organisms and can prevent water-borne infections.

name: UNIMI-IT
title: M.A.N.Z.O.N.I. — Microbial Approaches for Nanoparticles Zeroing and Optimizing Natural Integrity
abstract: 99% of people breathe polluted air. A large share of it is particulate matter, which is not one pollutant but a mixture of many. We engineer Escherichia coli MG1655 to absorb and process three of them: sulfate, nitrate and heavy metals. To overexpress whole pathways without plasmid burden, we built an integrative overexpressor: a λ-Red cassette combining a translation-enhancing MlcR 5′ UTR, an FRT-flanked kanamycin marker and one to five tandem Tac promoters, retargetable to any locus through 40 bp homology arms. With it we boosted the assimilatory sulfate pathway (cysNDC, cysJIH, plus cysZ, cysQ, trxA, cysG), nitrate uptake and reduction to ammonia (narU, narGHI, nirBD), and heavy-metal tolerance and bioaccumulation (sodA, zupT, and a synthetic operon pairing metallothionein ShMT3 with a periplasm-targeted OmpA–lead-binding peptide). Removal is quantified spectrophotometrically against wild type, supported by a model linking particle capture to metabolic kinetics.

name: UOregon
title: AquaFlock
abstract: Nitrogen fertilizers are an essential component of modern agriculture. Roughly half of applied nitrogen fertilizer is absorbed by plants; the rest gets converted into nitrate and leaches through the soil into ground and surface water. Elevated nitrate levels can harm ecosystems, contributing to eutrophication, and humans when nitrate-contaminated water is consumed. To address this issue, we engineered E. coli to sequester and store excess environmental nitrate within the cell. Nitrate gets converted into the nitrogen storage polymer cyanophycin; the bacteria start expressing flocculation proteins when a high concentration of cyanophycin is reached. The resulting flocs can be collected and used as fertilizer, recapturing the lost nutrients. We hope that this project will improve sustainability of nitrogen fertilization and reduce nitrogen pollution.

name: UOttawa
title: Nulfur: Sustainable Crude Oil Processing Through Engineered Biodesulfurization
abstract: 70% of crude oil is sour, rich in toxic sulfur compounds such as dibenzothiophene. Refineries remove these by hydrodesulfurization, an energy- and hydrogen-intensive process leaving spent catalyst as hazardous waste. Our project, Nulfur, develops a biodesulfurization alternative using the 4S pathway in engineered Pseudomonas putida. We developed Cofactor, an agentic AI tool guiding mutagenesis of bottleneck enzymes DszB and DszC. We sanitized broad-host-range plasmid pBBR1mcs-2 for Golden Gate assembly and confirmed expression in E. coli and P. putida. To optimize activity, we built and characterized modular Golden Gate-compatible promoter blocks spanning a graded expression range, designed a 24-member library tuning dszA–dszD, assembled eight, and detected desulfurization activity from one. Because metabolic burden caps single-strain throughput, we modelled a consortium where partner strains supply rhamnolipid and formate, relieving identified substrate-availability and NADH limits. Ultimately, Nulfur delivers cleaner oil processing while providing a framework for designing synthetic consortia for future applications.

name: UTArlington-TexasUSA
title: ForNever Chemicals: Bioelimination of Environmental Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS)
abstract:
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) persist in the environment and accumulate in organisms and food webs, raising concerns about ecological and human health. Unfortunately, the PFAS persistence is attributed to a number of highly stable Carbon-Fluorine bonds that hinder normal biological degradation of the PFA backbone. Rather than relying on effective but potentially harmful byproduct producing radical processes, our design involves the use of heterolytic enzymatic processes to safely ensure PFA bioremediation. 
Through the use of F19 vector ligated with 4 DNA fragments, crcB, dhaA, ssuE and fluoroacetate dehalogenase(FAcD), we aim to combine complementary enzymatic functions: breaking down carbon halogen bonds using FAcD, ssuE, and dhaA and removing toxic intracellular fluoride ion degradation products with crcB. Hence, this approach's goal is to understand whether this combination of DNA fragments can cause the defluorination and more complete degradation of PFAS within cells without generating unwanted partial breakdown products.

name: UVU-Utah
title: GreenARC: Atrazine Remediation by Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
abstract: Atrazine, a widely used herbicide, poses severe ecological threats. It exhibits high toxicity to aquatic life and amphibians and is recognized as an endocrine disruptor by the US EPA. Even though it is banned in over 60 nations, Atrazine remains widely used in other countries including the US, Canada, and Australia. Atrazine persists in soil for months or even years and eventually runs off into groundwater where it degrades at an even slower rate. The enzyme pathway AtzA-F has shown the ability to degrade atrazine into less harmful compounds. We aim to express these enzymes in the microalgae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, utilizing its ability to handle large genetic constructs and its resilience in aquatic and soil environments.

name: VIS
title: Cadture
abstract: Cadmium pollution is an environmental concern because of its harmful effects on human health and ecosystems. Detecting and removing cadmium requires expensive equipment or chemical treatments. In Project Cadture (Cadmium capture), we are developing an engineered Escherichia coli system that can both detect and capture cadmium. We built on a green fluorescent protein (GFP)-based cadmium detection system by introducing four metallothioneins (MTs). If any of the engineered MTs can capture cadmium, the GFP signal will decrease in comparison to the detection system, pMH45. When we monitored the bacterial culture in real time, we observed GFP intensity decrease compared to the sensor system, suggesting a decrease in cadmium concentration. We then expressed MTs in the cytoplasm. Bacteria with cytoplasmic MTs expressed very little GFP, suggesting that most cadmium was captured by MTs before activating GFP expression. Through this project, we demonstrate the potential of using MT-expressing bacteria to remove cadmium.

name: VIT-Vellore
title: Ammonia Capture Using a Glutamine Synthetase–PPK2 Coupled Cyclic Reaction System for Poultry Air Quality Management
abstract: Ammonia emissions arising from the microbial breakdown of uric acid and undigested proteins in poultry litter threaten poultry health, productivity, and air quality, causing respiratory damage and increasing disease susceptibility when concentrations exceed 20–25 ppm. To address this, the iGEM team of VIT-Vellore aims to develop a biosynthetic system that converts harmful gaseous ammonia into value-added glutamine. Using a feedback-resistant Bacillus subtilis glutamine synthetase coupled with a Sulfurovum lithotrophicum PPK2-mediated ATP regeneration cycle, ammonia is assimilated with glutamate (MSG), while MgCl₂, sodium polyphosphate, and ADP sustain a continuous ATP supply. This bio-based approach fixes ammonia into non-volatile glutamine, providing a sustainable alternative to chemical scrubbers and passive absorbents. Aligned with UN SDGs 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, and 17, Team VIT-Vellore promotes ethical, collaborative, and environmentally responsible biotechnology for sustainable poultry farming and improved environmental health.

name: WageningenUR
title: Triton: How to make the forever chemical forever no more!
abstract: Trifluoroacetate (TFA) is the shortest PFAS molecule, and the most overlooked. It circulates through our rivers, drinking water, and bodies. Long dismissed as harmless, there is now growing evidence for its hazardous effects on the environment and humans. Through feedback from our amazing stakeholders, we have identified how to tackle the root cause of the problem. Currently used techniques filter, but do not destroy TFA. That is why we have developed Triton. Triton is a holistic system that first concentrates TFA by binding it to a de novo TFA-binding protein attached to bacterial cellulose beads. Next, TFA flows into our bioreactor, where it is defluorinated by our evolved TFA dehalogenase. Here the TFA is broken down into harmless oxalate. Finally, to monitor the reduction in TFA concentration, we have designed a biosensor using a de novo TFA riboswitch. Together, these components combine to make the forever chemical forever no more!

name: WestviewHS SanDiego
title: Project PEARL: Protein Enabled Absorption and Recovery of rare earth eLements
abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) are critical for most modern technologies ranging from smartphones to wind turbines, yet the current extraction process often leaves behind contaminated water that conventional methods struggle to address. Metal-binding proteins from certain bacterial strains are candidates for a more environmentally-friendly possibility. In this project, we engineered Escherichia Coli to display metal binding proteins pedA1, mshA, and etfB on its outer surface to hopefully create a biological system that can capture REEs from contaminated water. Plasmids encoding these proteins were constructed with loop assembly and transformed into the E. Coli and were eventually tested using an Alizarin-based colorimetric assay to determine the efficiency of the proteins. Using this data, we wanted to see whether or not these proteins could possibly be utilized for the bioremediation of REEs.

name: WLSA-ShanghaiAcademy
title: ReLeaf: Converting Agricultural and Garden Waste into Bioethanol with Five Engineered Pichia pastoris Strains
abstract:
Garden waste, including leaves and branches, and agricultural residues, such as straw, corn cobs, and wheat stalks, are often burned or landfilled, causing air pollution, land consumption, and resource loss. ReLeaf aims to convert this lignocellulosic biomass into renewable bioethanol.

Using Pichia pastoris GS115 and the pPIC9K expression system, we produced five lignocellulose-degrading enzymes: laccase, endoglucanase, cellobiohydrolase, β-glucosidase, and xylanase. Measured activities included 1.66 U/mL for laccase, 2.58 U/mL for xylanase, and 0.283 U/mL total cellulase activity on Avicel. We also explored magnetic-bead-based enzyme recovery for potential reuse.

Our design combines enzymatic hydrolysis with yeast fermentation, using Saccharomyces cerevisiae to ferment glucose and engineered P. pastoris to utilize xylose. Across three Design–Build–Test–Learn cycles, we investigated enzyme production, biomass hydrolysis, and fermentation, assessing the feasibility of lignocellulosic waste valorization while emphasizing biosafety through cell-free enzyme preparations.

name: Worldshaper-Hangzhou
title: AirNova: An Enzyme-Powered Odor-Control Spray for Enclosed Public Spaces
abstract: Odor control is a critical challenge in crowded public spaces. Conventional methods, such as fragrance masking or chemical sprays, are often irritating and only temporary. To solve this, we engineered a bacterial system to produce a mix of natural enzymes that destroy bad smells at the molecular level. These enzymes break down foul-smelling compounds into completely odorless, non-volatile substances. Applied as a textile spray, the product remains on surfaces and is activated by ambient humidity to lock in and continuously degrade odors. This provides a safe, long-lasting, and sustainable biopurification solution for transit systems and shared indoor spaces.

name: YK Pao
title: The Golden Cicada’s Escape: A Smart-Sensing, Self-Floating Harvester for Heavy Metal Ions in Water
abstract: Heavy metal pollution in water, including lead, cadmium, and mercury, threatens ecosystems and human health. This project proposes a synthetic biology-based “capture-and-recovery” system using engineered E. coli BL21(DE3). A surface-display module, Lpp–OmpA–SmtA, is designed to bind extracellular metal ions, enhancing adsorption while reducing intracellular toxicity. Metal-responsive ZntR and PzntA regulation activates downstream functions in the presence of Zn²⁺, Cd²⁺, or Pb²⁺. Upon metal detection, the bacteria express antigen 43 (Ag43) to promote self-aggregation and gas-vesicle proteins (GVPs) to generate buoyancy. The cells are expected to form visible floating biorafts that can be collected with simple floating barriers or filters. By integrating sensing, adsorption, aggregation, and flotation, this system aims to enable low-cost, recoverable remediation of contaminated water while reducing secondary-pollution risks.

name: ABOA
title: Benzophe-none
abstract: Benzophenone-3 is an aromatic compound that has been commonly used in cosmetics, sunscreen and other items such as plastic as an UV filter. It is harmful to aquatic animals and coral because it is an endocrine disruptor. This has led to its use being reduced, but it is still used in controlled amounts in Asia, America and Europe. Since it is commonly used, harmful to the environment and current waste water treatment plants can’t remove it completely, we decided on a biological approach. Normal biological waste water treatment is inconsistent so our goal is to investigate a new proposed benzophenone breakdown pathway from Rhodococcus Oxybenzonivorans and try to incorporate it into current wastewater treatment plants. The pathway is new and experimental data is very limited. We chose to test two of the breakdown steps in E.coli to figure out how it could be used to remove benzophenone from waste water.

name: Alma
title: Com-BAT-ing White Nose Syndrome
abstract: Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd) is a pathogenic fungus responsible for White‑nose syndrome (WNS). Since its emergence, WNS has caused catastrophic declines in bat populations across North America. WNS develops during the bat hibernation period, when proteolytic enzymes produced by Pd degrade collagen in the nose, ears, and wings. This tissue damage forces bats to arouse prematurely from hibernation, triggering abnormal winter activity, rapid energy depletion, and ultimately death by starvation due to the absence of seasonal food resources. Despite the severity of this crisis, no effective large‑scale treatment currently exists. Our project proposes engineering Escherichia coli to secrete serine protease inhibitor(s) that target the key virulence factor (destructin-1) driving tissue degradation. By blocking collagen breakdown, these inhibitors would help bats maintain uninterrupted hibernation, improving survival outcomes and offering a promising biological strategy to protect one of our most essential ecological allies.

name: Athens
title: ApiconIASIS
abstract:
European Foulbrood is a bacterial disease of honeybee brood caused by Melissococcus plutonius. Infected larvae die before pupation, weakening or collapsing the colony. Across Europe control rests on destruction: past a defined level of infection the colony is destroyed and its frames burned. Antibiotics are unauthorised in the EU, no residue limit exists for honey, resistant strains are documented, and broad-spectrum treatment depletes the gut community that suppresses it.
ApiconIASIS is a targeted enzyme therapy from the pathogen’s own genome. Phages infecting M. plutonius encode endolysins, peptidoglycan hydrolases that evolved to lyse it. We screened published genomes for dormant prophages, ranked their lytic enzymes, and carried two forward. Both were expressed in Escherichia coli, purified, and assayed against a strain of reduced virulence; optical density fell. Neither acted on two honeybee gut commensals of the same order. The agent is a purified, non-replicating protein; the production strain stays contained.

name: BNUZH-China
title: PineProtector: An Engineered Bacillus subtilis Platform for Dual Control of Pine Wilt Disease
abstract: Pine wilt disease (PWD), caused by the pine-wood nematode (Bursaphelenchus xylophilus) and transmitted mainly by the Japanese pine sawyer (Monochamus alternatus), is a devastating forest disease; infected pines can wilt and die within 40 days. We propose PineProtector, a synthetic-biology-based platform that engineers Bacillus subtilis to colonize pine trunks and express two proteins with nematicidal and insecticidal activity against B. xylophilus and M. alternatus. Specifically, the engineered strain expresses the alkaline serine protease BLG4 under phenolic acid induced system to target nematodes and the Bacillus thuringiensis toxin Cry3Aa to target the vector insect. To ensure biosafety, a KillerRed-based suicide switch is incorporated: when the bacteria leave the pine interior and are exposed to sunlight, KillerRed produces ROS, which in turn trigger bacterial suicide. PineProtector is expected to provide a green, low-cost, and durable new strategy for the control of pine wilt disease, with the ultimate goal of protecting pine forests.

name: DNHS-SanDiego-Ca
title: Limiting Coral Bleaching By Targeting Pathogenic V. Coralliilyticus Using Engineered Bacterial Secretion of Phage-Derived Endolysin
abstract: Increased ocean temperatures are rapidly accelerating the severity of coral bleaching events worldwide. Thermal stress weakens coral immune defenses, triggers production of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS), and above 27°C, activates virulence in the pathogen Vibrio coralliilyticus, further harming the coral host. Current treatments struggle to target this pathogen without disrupting the coral holobiont. To address this, our team engineered coral symbiont Bacillus subtilis to secrete Lysdvp001, a phage-derived endolysin that lyses V. coralliilyticus, under a promoter activated by high concentrations of ROS, matching the conditions when the risk of virulence is the highest. Experimental validation demonstrated that our engineered coral probiotic remains comparable to a wild-type environment under low-stress conditions and inhibits V. coralliiyticus when exposed to ROS. Thus, we have created a proactive, biosensing intervention strategy that protects vulnerable coral ecosystems from pathogen-driven bleaching while preserving the natural balance of the coral holobiont.

name: GHCIS
title: ToeholdX: From AMR Detection to a Universal RNA Sensing Platform
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rapidly emerging as one of the greatest threats to global health. Resistance genes such as MCR-1, NDM-1, and KPC-2, which undermine last-resort antibiotics including colistin and carbapenems, are increasingly spreading through environmental pathways such as agricultural water systems. However, current detection methods rely on expensive instruments and specialized laboratories, making large-scale field surveillance difficult. To tackle this challenge, we developed a portable, low-cost diagnostic platform based on synthetic biology. Our system employs computationally designed RNA Toehold Switches to specifically recognize multiple antimicrobial resistance genes and generate distinct colorimetric outputs in a cell-free expression system. Coupled with RPA isothermal amplification and paper-based detection, the platform enables rapid, user-friendly, and equipment-free testing. By bringing AMR monitoring out of the laboratory and into the field, our project aims to support early warning, environmental surveillance, and more accessible public health protection.

name: GYHS
title: ReefBond: A Bifunctional Bioinspired Adhesive for Coral Reef Restoration
abstract: Secure attachment of coral fragments to the reef substrate remains a critical bottleneck in coral reef restoration. Conventional fixation strategies—cement, epoxy resins, and mechanical fasteners—face substantial limitations in underwater settings, including poor handling, long curing times, and the release of non-biodegradable materials into the marine environment. Inspired by mussel adhesion, the ReefBond project has designed and expressed a bifunctional fusion protein comprising mussel adhesive protein domains coupled to a mineralization-inducing peptide. Preliminary characterization demonstrates strong underwater adhesion and mineralization-promoting activity. Ongoing and future work will assess its adhesion performance and stability under marine conditions, its biodegradation profile, and its biocompatibility with coral tissue and other reef-associated organisms. By offering a biodegradable, bio-derived alternative to synthetic adhesives, ReefBond aims to provide a safer and more sustainable tool for coral outplanting and reef restoration, contributing to the protection of marine ecosystems.

name: HG-Tokyo
title: Recombinant Endolysin-royalisin for Invasive Gram-positive Neutralization (R.E.I.G.N.) - A Sustainable Strategy Against American Foulbrood
abstract: Honeybees are essential to the agricultural, food, and cosmetic industries, but their populations are increasingly threatened by American foulbrood (AFB), a highly contagious bacterial disease caused by Paenibacillus larvae. Current strategies require the destruction of infected hives, often through burning. To tackle this problem, we are leveraging royalisin, a natural antimicrobial peptide found in royal jelly. While royalisin exhibits activity against Gram-positive bacteria, P. larvae’s protective cell envelope and distinctive surface structures may hinder its effectiveness. To overcome this, we engineered a genetic construct in E. coli that produces genetically fused royalisin and P. larvae phage endolysin PlyPl23, creating a synergistic system that attacks the bacterium through complementary mechanisms. We envision application via a spray containing purified endolysin-royalisin together with uric acid and L-tyrosine, targeting both vegetative P. larvae cells and dormant endospores. By eliminating the pathogen without destroying colonies, we provide beekeepers a sustainable alternative to current control methods.

name: Hong Kong-CUHK
title: BeeTrix: A Self‑Sustaining Biocontrol System Against Varroa Mites
abstract: We are developing BeeTrix, a biological control system that leverages engineered Pseudomonas putida to continuously produce hop beta acids (lupulone) directly inside honeybee hives for sustainable Varroa mite management. Our biological system mimics a contact‑based killing mechanism, disrupting mite cellular ion balance and inducing oxidative stress with lupulone, without harming bees or contaminating honey. By using living bacteria as self‑renewing factories, BeeTrix overcomes the short half‑life of pure lupulone and eliminates the need for repeated chemical applications. Our aim is to create a single‑application, season‑long Varroa control solution that is safe, effective, and easily adopted by beekeepers worldwide.

name: IISER-Kolkata
title: FINS - Fish Intersex Neutralization Strategy
abstract: Estrogenic pollutants like estrone (E1) and 17β-estradiol (E2) enter waterways through wastewater, causing feminization, intersex conditions and fish population collapse. Our engineered E. coli carries two modules. The sensing and degradation module uses the EdcR repressor and its Pb promoter to detect estrogens, triggering a T7 RNA polymerase cascade that secretes BPUL laccase, which inactivates them by oligomer formation. The kill switch module expresses λ-phage Holin and T4 Endolysin to lyse the bacteria after treatment, preventing environmental release. We modelled the circuit deterministically and stochastically, and studied estrogen diffusion to test feasibility. Constants come from literature or multi-paper estimates, and sensitivity and error analyses support real-world use. For deployment, we designed tanks, columns and UV treatment tanks to neutralise runaway bacteria. Calculations, simulations and wet-lab experiments complemented one another, revealing the circuit's true behaviour.

name: IL Tech Chicago
title: SynBeeGee
abstract:
Honeybees are essential to agriculture and ecosystem health, yet pesticide exposure threatens their survival. Organophosphate pesticides can disrupt neurological function and contribute to declining colony health. SynBeeGee, developed by the Illinois Institute of Technology iGEM team, investigates a synthetic biology strategy to protect honey bees by engineering their native gut microbiome.
Our project focuses on Snodgrassella alvi, a bacterium naturally associated with the honey bee gut. By introducing genetic machinery for organophosphate degradation, we aim to enable this microorganism to break down harmful compounds and reduce pesticide exposure within its host. This approach could complement existing pollinator protection strategies without requiring farmers to abandon pest management practices.
SynBeeGee combines genetic engineering, laboratory experimentation, computational design, and stakeholder engagement to assess technical feasibility, biosafety, and practical implementation. Through collaboration with beekeepers, researchers, and agricultural stakeholders, the project explores how engineered microbial partnerships might support healthier colonies and more sustainable agricultural systems.

name: Lambert-GA
title: SWARM: Protecting the Hive
abstract:
Honeybee populations face a growing threat from Varroa destructor mites, which spread deformed wing virus (DWV), a major driver of colony losses worldwide. Between April 2024 and April 2025, U.S. beekeepers lost 55.6% of managed colonies, threatening pollinators essential to global agriculture.
Lambert iGEM developed SWARM, a two-step approach targeting both the virus and its vector. The first component is a de novo minibinder designed to neutralize DWV, the first experimentally validated binder against an iflavirus, designed at less than 1% of typical industry costs. The second is an RNA interference system targeting three genes critical to mite survival.
Supporting this work, we built PRINCE, a software for identifying favorable protein-binding regions, and Vapor-X, a low-cost hardware for vacuum-drying reagents. Through inclusive outreach and education, SWARM advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and supports a sustainable future for global pollinators.

name: Nanjing-China
title: PhosArmor
abstract:
Metal corrosion reduces the service life of equipment, generates solid waste, and necessitates frequent anti-corrosion treatments for metallic components. However, traditional metal anti-corrosion methods often cause environmental pollution.  PhosArmor explores a synthetic biology approach to corrosion protection that prioritizes environmental health. We engineered *Shewanella oneidensis* MR-1 to overexpress *phoU*, a gene encoding a regulator of phosphate homeostasis, to promote protective mineralization on metal surfaces. Comparative strain testing, electrochemical characterization, and mineral analysis support its potential for corrosion protection under laboratory conditions. We also designed a light-controlled kill switch intended to enable strain elimination after mineralization, pending functional validation. 
By combining biologically driven surface protection with biocontainment design, PhosArmor aims to reduce corrosion-related material waste and dependence on chemically intensive maintenance. The project provides a foundation for developing more sustainable wastewater infrastructure management.

name: NU Boston
title: Soil Shield
abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) persist in soil and can bioaccumulate, posing risks to agricultural, environmental, and urban systems. To solve this problem, we developed a bacterial bioremediation system by engineering Pseudomonas Putida KT2440 to degrade naphthalene, a representative PAH, in dry, post-wildfire soil conditions, where analogous soil bacteria die. We investigated a salicylate-dependent kill-switch with flow cytometry methods and assessed salicylate degradation and the effectiveness of hydroxyectoine as an osmoprotectant with plate-reader assays and a purpose-built soil chamber. We also designed biodegradable alginate beads for bacterial delivery into soil and created an application to define environmental conditions and map pollution to optimize deployment of our bacteria.

name: NWAFU-China
title: AMPlify: AI-Designed Antimicrobial Peptides for Animal Health and Conservation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance demands new approaches that balance antibacterial activity, host compatibility, and environmental responsibility. Inspired by dairy-goat mastitis management, AMPlify integrates AI-guided antimicrobial peptide design with experimental validation and a One Health perspective. Our generative model, TAM-Flow, generated 10,000 sequences, from which seven candidates underwent molecular dynamics simulations and in vitro evaluation. Three candidates exhibited relatively broad antibacterial activity within the tested strain panel, while hemolysis and cytotoxicity assays informed iterative refinement. Recombinant production yielded a fraction with antibacterial activity. Complementary software evaluates peptide properties and explores degradation, environmental fate, and resistance pressure. Stakeholder engagement shaped research priorities, while multilingual materials and interactive games supported public education. Together, AMPlify connects computational discovery, experimental evidence, production research, and societal needs to support responsible development of antimicrobial peptides for animal health.

name: Peking
title: TermiTox: Engineered Yeast for Targeted Biocontrol of Termites in Wooden Heritage Conservation
abstract: Historic timber structures across China—palaces, temples, and old residences—are threatened by termites which cause hidden damage that undermines their preservation. Current control relies on chemical pesticides, which persist and harm non-target organisms. In our iGEM project, we engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a bait-based delivery chassis; termites acquire it from a contained station and spread it via trophallaxis. Guided by termite life history—wood digestion relies on the termite and its gut protists—we designed two complementary modules: a pH-sensitive H311A LLO variant that targets gut protists, and an RNAi module with two single-hairpin constructs targeting RsEG (cellulase) and Hexamerin-1 (caste regulation). A glucanase-assisted release module aids payload escape. Biosafety is enforced by hypoxia- and acetate-responsive promoters, sequence specificity, and physical containment. Overall, TermiTox aims to provide targeted, modular, and environmentally responsible termite control for wooden heritage and forest ecosystems.

name: RDFZ-China
title: GlacierGuard: Engineering a biodegradable bacterial cellulose material for glacier protection via water retention
abstract:
Glacier retreat is accelerating under global climate change, threatening ecosystems and water resources. Existing glacier-covering materials are mainly made from plastics or synthetic fibers, which may cause secondary pollution after long-term use.
Our project aims to develop a biodegradable glacier-protection material based on bacterial cellulose (BC). Owing to its high water-retention capacity, BC can absorb and retain meltwater during the daytime. Under low nighttime temperatures, the retained water can refreeze, reducing net ice loss and helping preserve glacier mass. Produced by engineered microorganisms, BC is renewable, environmentally friendly, and biodegradable.
By utilizing the natural water-holding properties of bacterial cellulose, this project seeks to provide a sustainable bio-based strategy for mitigating glacier melting and protecting vulnerable glacier ecosystems.

name: REC-CHENNAI
title: THULIR – Technology for Harnessing Unique stress-responsive proteins for Long-term Integrated conservation of Recalcitrant seeds
abstract: Seeds are the lifeline of plants, facilitating their propagation and conservation. Orthodox seeds, such as rice, beans can withstand conventional seed banking methods, remain viable for extended periods. In contrast, recalcitrant seeds are highly sensitive to dehydration and freezing, making their long-term preservation challenging, endangering the conservation of ecologically important plant species. This is due to high expression of Late Embryogenesis-Abundant (LEA) proteins in orthodox seeds where it protects the seeds from stress. THULIR provides a solution by engineering the LEA domains with metal ion binding motif and a cell-penetrating peptide, that facilitates their delivery into the embryonic axis of the Artocarpus heterophyllus seeds. LEA proteins are engineered with pET (blank) vector and expressed in E. coli BL21, purified through His-tag/Ni-NTA column chromatography. Once delivered, the engineered LEA proteins enhance the cryo-stress tolerance and improve their survival without modifying the plant genome, facilitating a sustainable strategy for long-term cryopreservation.

name: Shanghai-city
title: Sentinel of Light Pollution: Fluorescent Biosensors for Sensing Light Pollution
abstract: Light pollution is an increasingly severe global environmental problem, disrupting circadian rhythms of organisms and destabilizing ecosystems. Traditional light detectors rely on electronic hardware, which are costly and lack biological relevance to reflect how living organisms perceive light signals. Our project develops fluorescent biosensors as biological sentinels to detect light pollution.

name: UNILausanne
title: Detect, Disarm, Defend: A Multi-Layered Strategy Against the Crayfish Plague
abstract: Crayfish plague, caused by Aphanomyces astaci, has pushed native European crayfish toward extinction. Invasive North American crayfish spread the pathogen while remaining resistant. Guided by discussions with experts and stakeholders, we developed a multi-layered strategy. Detect: We developed a LAMP (loop-mediated isothermal amplification) assay for in-field monitoring, validated for specificity, sensitivity, and robustness, and built a portable incubator to run LAMP in the field. Disarm: We propose RNA interference to silence genes encoding KPI2 and KPILA, which confer resistance in the invasive host. We engineered the necessary double-stranded RNA-producing plasmids and showed that four terminators on either side of the gene significantly increased dsRNA yield. Defend: We cloned, expressed, and purified KPI2 and KPILA, hypothesizing that exogenous delivery could improve native crayfish survival. We adapted a water-in-oil-in-water emulsion into alginate-chitosan feed beads for oral delivery. Together, this multi-layered strategy equips us to preserve native crayfish in Swiss rivers and lakes.

name: UZurich
title: SeisMIC - UZurich 2026: Stabilizing the soil ahead of us
abstract:
Shallow landslides threaten settlements, infrastructure, and ecosystems in the Swiss Alps. SeisMIC investigates microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) as a potential approach to stabilising shallow alpine soils. Our project addresses three main challenges: bacterial activity at low temperatures, controlled calcium carbonate precipitation, and environmental impacts.

In the wet lab, we investigated directed evolution of Sporosarcina pasteurii (S. pasteurii) for cold adaptation and strategies to regulate urease expression and carbonate formation. Cold-adapted populations showed shorter lag phases under cold conditions and retained qualitative precipitation ability. Engineered Escherichia coli strains exhibited induction-associated urease responses, while carbonic anhydrase results remained open. 

Complementary models explored slope stability and treatment feasibility, while Human Practices integrated stakeholder perspectives. SeisMIC establishes a foundation for further research, highlighting the need to validate treatment efficacy, environmental safety, and practical applicability before real-world deployment.

name: Aalto-Helsinki
title: DAHLIA: Making Food Safety Visible
abstract: Is your food safe to eat? Earlier this year, Finnish broadcasters exposed issues with the storage of meat and fish in supermarkets. The Aalto-Helsinki iGEM team presents DAHLIA, a test strip that detects the histamine emitted by foods like meat and fish as they spoil. In our biosensor, Diamine Oxidase (DAO) reacts with histamine, producing H2O2, and Horseradish Peroxidase (HRP) reacts with H2O2 and changes the color of a substrate. DAO and HRP are each joined to a cellulose-binding module (CBM) to adhere to the cellulose-based test strip. Our team successfully designed, transformed and expressed both fusion proteins and developed assays for prototype testing. To ensure the positive impact of the product on our community, we interacted with consumers, food vendors, and experts from different fields. We especially strived to educate the community about food safety and histamine - for a future with less food waste and more food safety.

name: Anatolia College-GR
title: Engineering Chlorella Vulgaris to Enhance Non-Heme Iron Bioavailability
abstract: Iron deficiency continues to be one of the most prevalent nutritional concerns worldwide, particularly impacting populations that depend on plant-based diets abundant in non-heme iron, which has low bioavailability. Our initiative, Engineering Chlorella vulgaris to Enhance Non-Heme Iron Bioavailability, tackles this issue through the application of synthetic biology by genetically modifying the microalgae Chlorella Vulgaris to overexpress the VTC2/GGP gene, a crucial enzyme in the L-ascorbic acid biosynthesis pathway. By significantly increasing the production of vitamin C within the organism, we seek to naturally improve iron absorption in the same context. Transgenic strains will be created using electroporation, and their effectiveness will be assessed through in-vitro digestion models. Ultimately, our aim is to develop an affordable and sustainable algae-based capsule supplement, bridging the divide between metabolic engineering and global nutritional security.

name: BOKU-Vienna
title: Algaeneering
abstract:
Micronutrient deficiencies affect billions worldwide. Our project aimed to establish a proof of concept for vitamin overproduction in microalgae by engineering Chlamydomonas reinhardtii to increase vitamin C and folate production through overexpression of GGP, GTPCHI, and ADCS.
Through expert and stakeholder interviews, we questioned our approach, its potential benefits, and the challenges of genetically modified foods. They also highlighted that technology can only deliver real impact when paired with trust and public acceptance. This strengthened our focus on education and public engagement.
Computational models complemented our laboratory work by exploring biological processes relevant to vitamin production. Experimentally, we confirmed reporter expression and obtained promising preliminary results for transformation with our GGP construct, while successful transformation of the folate constructs remains unconfirmed.
Although further research is needed, our project provides a starting point for developing vitamin-enriched microalgae and demonstrates the importance of combining experimental research, computational modeling, and public engagement.

name: Bonn
title: PotyGuard⁺ - A bodyguard for your vegetable yard
abstract:
PotyGuard⁺ is a modular, protease-responsive biosensor designed to detect viral infection in plant cells and convert viral protease activity into a programmable cellular response. The system combines split proteins, Npu DnaE inteins, and inhibitory peptide cages that prevent spontaneous reconstitution. Protease-mediated cage removal enables the split components to reassemble and restore protein function.

We demonstrated the functionality of this architecture using split eGFP as a fluorescent proof of concept in Nicotiana benthamiana. The same principle can be transferred to functional effectors, such as split Cre recombinase, linking protease activity to downstream cellular responses.

By separating sensing from output, PotyGuard⁺ can be adapted to different proteases and effectors. This enables applications ranging from fluorescence and recombinase activity to transcriptional or signaling responses. Such outputs could conditionally constitute a defense against viral replication or restrict viral spread in plants, while the underlying architecture provides a broadly applicable platform for protease-responsive synthetic biology.

name: Cataverse-Beijing
title: A Portable Rapid Bacterial Detection System Mediated by Cerium-Based MOF Nanozymes
abstract: Foodborne pathogens can be transmitted through contaminated media such as vegetables, causing a range of illnesses from mild diarrhea, abdominal pain, and vomiting to severe fever and even hemolytic uremic syndrome. These pathogens pose a persistent threat to public health security. Therefore, the development of rapid and sensitive detection methods for foodborne pathogens is of great practical significance for early warning and effective prevention of foodborne diseases. To address this need, we have developed a novel rapid bacterial detection platform based on magnetic bead–phage receptor-binding protein coupling technology, a cerium-based MOF nanozyme (Ce-UiO-66) with alkaline phosphatase-like activity, and a smartphone application. This platform provides promising technical support for food safety monitoring, primary-level public health protection, and on-site rapid diagnosis.

name: Cataverse-Shanghai
title: Reshaping the Future of Food: Unlocking the Nutritional Secrets of Novel Plant Proteins
abstract: With the growth of the global population, rising health awareness and increasing demand for sustainable development, plant proteins have become a key development direction in the food industry due to their advantages of abundant resources, environmental friendliness and balanced nutrition. In the field of plant based meat products, plant proteins can mimic the texture, mouthfeel and flavor of animal meat through protein modification, compounding technologies and processing process optimization, meeting consumers’ demands for health, environmental protection and diversification. This project selects potato glycoprotein Patatin, hemp seed protein Edestin 1 and cassava 11S globulin as core raw materials for improving the mouthfeel of plant based meat. Heterologous expression is performed using the Pichia pastoris platform, aiming to provide safe and controllable high quality protein raw materials and replicable synthetic biology solutions for sustainable food systems.

name: CAU-China
title: Fungal Sentinel
abstract:
Globally, approximately 3% of grain is lost to mold annually, with China losing 42 billion kg in storage. Since visual inspection and laboratory tests typically detect contamination only after fungal growth has occurred, CAU-China 2026 introduces Fungal Sentinel, a yeast-based platform designed to sense fungal volatile organic compounds (VOCs) —specifically 1-octen-3-ol, a key biomarker of mold—before visible contamination appears.
Our sensor rewires the yeast mating pathway: an olfactory receptor (OR) binds the VOC, a Gpa1–Gαolf chimera relays the signal, and the FUS1 promoter drives ymStayGold, converting ligand binding into a measurable green fluorescence output.
For readout, OptiX, a phone-based fluorimeter costing about $15 in materials, resolves the reporter spectrum from RAW images down to nanomolar levels. Together, the living sensor and the pocket reader transform invisible, early-stage contamination into a measurable signal long before mold becomes visible.

name: Chalmers-Gothenburg
title: CHYMERA: Cell-Based Hybrid Yeast system for Multi-analyte Engineered Receptor Assays
abstract: Biogenic amines such as histamine and tyramine accumulate during microbial food spoilage and represent important indicators for example scombroid poisoning. The aim of this project was to create a yeast-based biosensor, detecting histamine and tyramine, in order to facilitate the detection of spoiled fish prior to consumption. The human GPCRs, H3HR and TAAR1 as well as the honeybee (Apis mellifera) orthologues amTAR1 and amTAR2 were cloned using MoClo assembly and expressed in S. cerevisiae. The receptor genes were introduced into Ste2/Ste3 (-mating factor receptor) knockout strains. The strains contained a modified MAPK cascade together with Gαi3/Gpa1 chimeric G protein α -subunit and Ste12LexA chimeric transcription factor with a GFP reporter gene coupled to the LexO6xLEU2 promoter. Membrane localization of BFP-fused receptors was studied using fluorescence microscopy indicating secondary vacuolar and ER localization. Functional analysis of ligand interaction indicated that the biosensor was non-functional under the tested conditions.

name: China SUIS GB
title: Fish Spoilage Biosensor
abstract:
Seafood spoilage generates significant global food waste, primarily driven by fish degrading into volatile organic compounds like trimethylamine (TMA). To combat this, we developed a biosensor engineered for cold-chain environments (0–4°C) that detects gaseous TMA.
Our system utilizes a two-strain Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 co-culture. Strain 1 contains a cold-inducible promoter PcspA, expressing periplasmic TMM, converting incoming gaseous TMA to TMAO. Strain 2 senses extracellular TMAO through its native periplasmic TorT/TorS machinery, initiating a phosphorylation cascade that activates the Ptor promoter to express the blue chromoprotein AmilCP.
Across two engineering cycles, we conducted double digestion (PstI/SacI) and ligation molar ratios (5:1 insert-to-vector) using plasmids pDSK519 and pBBR1MCS-1. PCR cross-validation confirmed successful strain construction and plasmid maintenance under selective antibiotics. Finally, we integrated this co-culture into a dual-layer product featuring an outer gas-permeable cellulose acetate shell and inner porous agarose microbeads for bacterial immobilization.

name: DEPU
title: Degradation of Acrylamide in High-Temperature-Processed Foods Using Immobilized Dual-Enzyme Systems
abstract: Acrylamide, a probable human carcinogen, is widely produced in thermally processed foods via the Maillard reaction between asparagine and reducing sugars. Natural enzymes suffer from low thermostability and fail to work efficiently under high-temperature food processing conditions. To solve this and the limitations of single-enzyme approaches and high costs, we build an immobilized dual-enzyme system of L-asparaginase and glucose oxidase. LEA peptides are applied to greatly boost enzyme thermostability, and food-grade crosslinkers enable co-immobilization to remove two key precursors. This eco-friendly, recyclable solution effectively reduces acrylamide in fried and baked foods and improves public food safety.

name: HKSSC
title: Waste-to-watt: Engineering PrbA for Enhanced Food Waste Bioenergy Production
abstract: While industrial anaerobic digestion converts tonnes of global food waste into renewable bioenergy, a critical hidden bottleneck lowers efficiency: synthetic preservatives like parabens accumulate in waste streams, paralyze functional microbes. So we, HKSSC introduces Waste-to-Watt, a targeted solution designed to overcome this industrial crisis. By engineering E. coli to express the paraben-degrading enzyme prbA, our system neutralizes chemical inhibitors to accelerate microbial digestion. Grounded in rigorous engineering design, modeling, and wet-lab validation, Waste-to-Watt bridges molecular innovation with municipal green infrastructure, maximizing renewable energy yields and establishing scalable blueprint for sustainable global waste valorization. We have charactereized 16 new parts, including 14 new basic parts and 2 new composite parts. Furthermore, through our structured iCycle Integrated Human Practices framework and extensive community outreach in all age groups, including school workshops, interactive games, and public surveys, we engaged diverse stakeholders to guide project optimization while inspiring the next generation of synthetic biologists.

name: Hongwen School
title: BrewXOS: A Solution for Transforming Brewer's Spent Grain into High-Value Prebiotics
abstract:
Brewing generates approximately 38 million tonnes of brewer’s spent grain (BSG) annually, largely used as low-value animal feed. Converting its fibre into potential prebiotic ingredients could create greater economic value through functional food applications. However, complex fibre structures and separate enzyme-production steps complicate conversion.
BrewXOS engineers Bacillus subtilis with three complementary enzymes to combine enzyme production and BSG conversion in one fermentation process, without adding purified enzymes. After 12 hours, our best strain achieved a control-adjusted sugar yield of 107.9 mg xylose equivalents per gram of dry BSG, with further evidence of oligosaccharide-like products. We also built a compact fermentation-monitoring prototype and incorporated stakeholder feedback into ingredient development.
Future work will identify and recover the products, validate safety and prebiotic function, and evaluate food compatibility and production economics—advancing spent grain toward ingredients with nutritional and economic potential.

name: Jilin-China
title: NutriTrace: A Living DNA Recorder for Fermentation
abstract: Fermented products including beer, wine, soy sauce, cheese and many yeast-derived ingredients are manufactured in large stirred tanks. Poor mixing and uneven mass transfer form gradients of nutrients, oxygen and metabolites, generating local microenvironmental stresses that reduce yield. Conventional detection averages tank conditions into one value and fails to capture these stresses. We constructed a living DNA recorder in Komagataella phaffii. Cells permanently record their experienced stresses into DNA, and this stress history can be read out by fluorescence after fermentation. Each recording channel combines a stress-responsive promoter and a site-specific recombinase; the target stress is defined by the promoter, making the recorder adaptable to different industrial processes. Encapsulated in calcium-cross-linked alginate beads, engineered cells are recoverable for post-run readout. Unlike real-time probes showing instant fermenter status, our recorder records each cell’s past exposure, providing engineers with information for process adjustment.

name: JZIB-QDHS
title: A New Herbal Approach to Weight Loss: Functional Foods Targeting SULT Enzymes
abstract: This project targets human sulfotransferases (SULT2B1, SULT1E1, SULT2A1) involved in metabolic regulation. Using a fluorescence-based high-throughput screening platform, natural compounds are screened via molecular docking and validated for SULT inhibition. Synergistic inhibitor combinations are identified using Chou-Talalay analysis. A dual-enzyme biosynthesis system (UGT88D4 + UGD) is engineered in E. coli to produce bioactive flavonoid glycosides. The final formulation is tested in 3T3-L1 adipocyte differentiation models for reduced lipid accumulation and adipogenic gene expression. This work provides a functional food strategy for weight management.

name: KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei
title: Herculyeast
abstract: Taiwan is ending food waste pig feeding due to African Swine Fever policies, with a final transition deadline in December, 2026, leaving stored waste that can clog plumbing, produce odors, and contribute to climate change through methane release. To address this, we engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae to secrete two digestive enzymes: Proteinase A (PEP4) for protein degradation and sterol esterase (TGL1) for lipid degradation. Fusion to the MFα1 prepro-leader sequence is intended to redirect both enzymes into the culture medium, under inducible and constitutive promoters. Enzymes collected from the medium are intended to power two products: a two-chamber reactor that sequentially degrades lipids and proteins and an enzyme-based drain unblocker that targets grease buildup. Because both products use enzyme preparations rather than live engineered yeast, they are intended to treat food waste at its source as pretreatment before conventional treatment. We hope this pretreatment reduces storage needs and eases environmental impacts.

name: KhanLab-BayArea
title: The Cluck is Ticking
abstract:
Globally, meat waste accounts for approximately 100 billion USD of lost value annually. A major driver of this waste is the reliance on static expiration dates, which disregard real-world variability during storage and handling. Consequently, meat is often disposed of prematurely at every level of the supply chain. More importantly, spoiled meat is consumed unintentionally posing serious individual and public health risks. 

To address this issue, we are engineering an E. coli based biosensor to detect cadaverine, a metabolic byproduct of bacteria that accumulates in meat over time. Our biosensor will produce more chromoprotein in response to increased concentrations of cadaverine. In parallel, we will develop a mathematical model to predict live-response meat expiration dates, allowing consumers, producers, and sellers to make clear choices about food conservation and consumption.

name: Kyoto
title: OiLipase
abstract: Rice bran rapidly degrades after milling due to lipase-driven free fatty acid (FFA) production. We developed OiLipase, a two-part system to combat this: KANNAME, a spatiotemporally controlled protease system that selectively degrades the lipase at the oil-water interface and self-inactivates via a timed split-protease mechanism; and NIINAME, a cell-free FFA biosensor adapted from the ROSALIND platform. Together, they enable heat-free control and monitoring of rice bran rancidity.

name: Latvia-Riga
title: TRACE – Trichinella Rapid Assay for Capture-to-Consumption Evaluation.
abstract: Trichinellosis persists as a zoonotic barrier at the intersection of wildlife ecology and human food safety. The standard regulatory method, artificial pepsin digestion, is tethered to centralized laboratories, requiring specialized equipment and extensive processing. This dependency creates a diagnostic void for remote populations and hunters consuming wild game without veterinary oversight. Project TRACE bridges this gap with a decentralized, field-ready screening platform. Its architecture leverages Bacillus subtilis spore display, fusing passenger proteins and biotin acceptor-peptides to native CotB, CotC and CotG coat proteins, with sfGFP as a size placeholder for VHH-nanobodies against the T. spiralis serine protease. This yields a durable, shelf-stable bioreagent, while an Fe-EDTA-ethanol protocol renders spores non-viable before release. Bypassing hazardous acids, sample preparation uses a detergent-buffer and mechanical maceration to isolate antigens into a liquid exudate. Detection is via lateral flow assay, visualizing spore-antigen complexes with streptavidin-coated carbon nanoparticles.

name: NPSI Singapore
title: ProbioRegulon
abstract: As diabetes becomes one of the world’s largest health challenges, interest has grown in food-based approaches to managing blood glucose. Bitter gourd (Momordica charantia) has long been used for this purpose, and contains mcIRBP-19, a peptide reported to act at the insulin receptor. But the amount present in the plant varies with variety, ripeness and preparation, and the natural sequence is under patent. In our project, we redesigned the peptide and had the coding sequences synthesised, then verified the resulting constructs in bacteria, working toward secretion from Lactobacillus paracasei, a food-grade probiotic. Delivering the peptide from bacteria living in the gut avoids the main obstacle facing peptides taken by mouth, which are largely broken down before they can act. Computational modelling guided every design decision. In the future, Mordilac could become a palatable probiotic drink, offering a familiar food format for people managing or at risk of type 2 diabetes.

name: NTHU
title: AeroSense: A Modular Biohybrid Olfactory Platform for Agricultural Screening
abstract: Fungal deterioration causes substantial crop losses, highlighting the need for accessible tools for early, on-site detection. Our project, AeroSense, is a modular biohybrid olfactory platform designed for agricultural screening, with banana production as its intended first application. The platform brings together a cell-based sensing array expressing Drosophila odorant receptors and ORCO in HEK293 cells, GCaMP6f fluorescence reporting, a four-channel optical reader, and a fly-inspired neural network for odor-pattern decoding. We documented reporter expression and conducted exploratory measurements of fluorescence kinetics. We built and tested the optical reader using fluorescent standards, with transport and optical modeling informing its design. Computational studies evaluated odor-pattern decoding on external sensor datasets. Discussions with agricultural researchers and potential users shaped the proposed screening workflow and a shared-access deployment strategy. With reusable analysis code, hardware documentation, and educational resources, this work lays the groundwork for an accessible screening tool to guide follow-up inspection and confirmatory testing.

name: NYCU-Taiwan
title: BITE: Biosensing for Instant Target Pathogen Evaluation
abstract:
Foodborne pathogens threaten public health, yet conventional detection often requires specialized equipment, trained personnel, and time-consuming procedures. To make preliminary food safety screening more accessible, we developed BITE (Biosensing for Instant Target Pathogen Evaluation), a synthetic biology-based platform designed for intuitive visual detection.

Using Salmonella invA DNA as a proof-of-concept target, BITE combines magnetic bead-based DNA enrichment, CRISPR-Cas12a molecular recognition, and G-quadruplex–hemin (G4–hemin) DNAzyme colorimetric readout. Magnetic beads capture and concentrate target DNA, Cas12a provides sequence-specific recognition, and the G4–hemin system generates a visible blue signal through TMB oxidation.

We investigated these modules experimentally and used mathematical modelling to study detection processes. Industry consultations provided technical and product-development perspectives, while educational outreach promoted synthetic biology. By integrating molecular recognition with a simple visual readout, BITE explores a portable approach to preliminary foodborne pathogen screening.

name: Okinawa
title: pHlex
abstract:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical problem in human and veterinary medicine, driven largely by antibiotic overuse. We focused on two bacteria for which resistance is becoming serious. Brachyspira hyodysenteriae, the agent of swine dysentery, is endemic in Okinawa, Japan, where pigs are often given multiple antibiotics over long periods, disrupting the gut microbiota and weakening immunity; simple antibiotic-free control measures are therefore needed on farms. Helicobacter pylori infects 4.4 billion people and causes gastric cancer, with high-risk strains common in Japan, China, and South Korea, and resistant strains are emerging.

We aim to develop phage therapy against these gastrointestinal pathogens. Because phages are inactivated by gastric acid after oral administration, we constructed an original AI platform to predict genetic sequences conferring acid resistance. Guided by these predictions, acid-resistant phage strains will be engineered into new preparations effective against B. hyodysenteriae and H. pylori.

name: OUC-China
title: Pro-TPSP : Engineering a Programmable and Tunable Platform for Tailored Pullulan
abstract:
Pullulan is a biodegradable microbial polysaccharide with potential applications in edible films, food packaging, nutritional products, and animal-free capsule shells. These applications require different film-forming properties and viscosities, both closely related to molecular weight.
Pro-TPSP aims to develop a programmable platform for tailoring pullulan properties in Aureobasidium melanogenum P16. We target AmyR, a shared regulator of three hydrolase genes, through two complementary approaches: a Tet-On system enabling externally induced transcriptional control, and uORF-mediated translational regulation guided by sequence-based models and evaluated through two rounds of GFP reporter assays. These approaches explore control over pullulan molecular weight and viscosity. Preliminary results showed that combining the selected A1444 uORF with amyR increased pullulan molecular weight relative to parental P16. By connecting expression regulation with material requirements, our project offers a strategy for developing customized biomaterials for future food and nutrition applications.

name: RooseveltSATX
title: Amisense
abstract: One of the challenges in preventing food-related illnesses from fish stems from their rapid decomposition—which can occur before there are any sensory cues such as unpleasant odors and visual changes. Microbial degradation and autolysis starts on the molecular level with the production of compounds through chemical reactions—such as the bioamine 'histamine'. Our team seeks to address this global food safety issue by creating an accessible and authentic product that detects contamination before reaching the consumer. By engineering DNA, our team has created a color changing biosensor that detects rising histamine levels before any physical manifestations show.

name: SCU-China
title: DunaTerp:  A Programmable Carotenoid Metabolic Platform
abstract:
Terpenoids supply most natural food pigments and flavors, yet plant extraction suffers from low yield and high cost, while synthetic alternatives raise safety concerns. We developed DunaTerp, a food-grade terpenoid platform using Dunaliella salina — the only industrially cultivated microalga for natural β-carotene. D. salina already possesses a complete endogenous MEP pathway and efficiently expresses LCYB, natively accumulating β-carotene up to 14% of dry weight and bypassing costly precursor engineering.
We introduce CPP transcription factors that simultaneously activate β-carotene synthesis and suppress competing branches, redirecting flux toward a shared β-carotene hub. Building on this hub, modular pipelines produce astaxanthin (BKT), β-ionone (CCD1), crocetin (GjCCD4a/GjALDH2C3), and β-citraurin (CitCCD4). For biocontainment, a salt-dependent mazE-mazF switch triggers cell death upon escape into low-salt environments. Interchangeable enzyme cassettes allow flexible adaptation to diverse terpenoid products, making DunaTerp a generalizable chassis for sustainable terpenoid supply.

name: SHSBNU-China
title: BLISS: Bioengineered Low-calorie Innovative Sweetener Synthesis
abstract: Current sugar substitutes often compromise taste and deprive people joy of eating. The sweet protein Brazzein, from Pentadiplandra brazzeana, combines a clean, sugar-like taste with promising stability during processing. However, difficulties with protein folding and purification in recombinant microbial expressions limit its production for broader commercial use. BLISS addresses these challenges through a novel active inclusion body strategy in Escherichia coli. Using the SAP peptide (L6KD) and partner adapter tags (Sumo and MtuI), we demonstrated improved Brazzein production and simplified its recovery. With AI-assisted protein engineering, we identified variants with potentially better stability and sweetness. We also evaluated expression in yeast for scalable, food-grade production. Through iterative engineering, we develop PrintScope, a figure-sized miniature microscope, to promote accessible biology education. Ultimately, BLISS seeks to create a sweet future without the associated health burden.

name: SSBS
title: Enabling “Slow Absorption” of Starch: Reconstructing Low-Glycemic Index (GI) Resistant Starch via a Multi-Enzyme System
abstract: With the widespread prevalence of metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and obesity worldwide, their rapid digestion and high glycemic index (GI)—have become increasingly prominent. Resistant starch (RS), as a food ingredient that combines the benefits of a low GI with dietary fiber, has emerged as a key focus in healthy dietary interventions. Based on the principles of synthetic biology and multi-enzyme synergistic catalysis, this study established a three-enzyme synergistic modification system comprising hydrolysis, chain elongation, and debranching (α-amylase, 4-α-glucan transferase, and pullulanase). to specifically reconfigure the molecular structure and crystalline properties of starch. The modification effects were evaluated through experiments such as SEM analysis and resistant starch (RS) content determination. Ultimately, a low-GI resistant starch preparation process suitable for daily staple foods such as noodles and bread was developed, providing a feasible dietary intervention strategy for patients with metabolic diseases and individuals seeking weight management.

name: Tec-Chihuahua
title: BruSafe: mRNA platform for bovine brucellosis prevention
abstract: Bovine brucellosis, caused mainly by Brucella abortus, remains one of the most widespread neglected zoonoses, endemic in Mexico, where 57.4% of national territory is still in the control phase. Current vaccines rely on live attenuated strains: S19 interferes with serological diagnosis, while RB51 is abortifacient, shed in milk, virulent and rifampicin-resistant in humans, and less protective than claimed. We present BruSafe, a non-replicating vaccine platform in which an mRNA encoding a multiepitope antigen derived from conserved Brucella outer membrane proteins (OMP10, OMP25, OMP25b) is packaged into a 27 nm self-assembling MS2 bacteriophage virus-like particle produced in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3). The particle contains no live organism, no smooth lipopolysaccharide and no antibiotic-resistance marker, making it DIVA-compatible, safe in pregnant cattle and cold-chain tolerant. Subcutaneously delivered, it targets dendritic cells to elicit the CD4⁺ Th1/IFN-γ response required for protection, and its modular cassette is retargetable to other pathogens.

name: Texas
title: Engineering Probiotics to Combat Malnutrition
abstract: Malnutrition affects millions worldwide, and a subset of children fail to respond to microbiota-directed complementary foods (MDCFs). Recent work links this to absence of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, whose FAAH enzyme hydrolyzes oleoylethanolamide (OEA), a lipid messenger signaling satiety and suppressing food intake. We engineered Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 to express a transmembrane-domain-deleted FAAH fused to YebF. Unexpectedly, YebF localized it to the bacterial membrane instead of secreting, reconstituting FAAH to it’s native compartment. We confirmed membrane localization and demonstrated OEA hydrolysis by the engineered strain. In parallel, MICOM community metabolic modeling reproduced the gut’s known cross-feeding network from genome content alone and found OEA absent from shared bacterial metabolism, consistent with a host-derived signal. Integrated human practices with researchers, clinicians, NGOs and community leaders, plus webinars, $3 meal plans and a gated deployment route, grounded the work. This offers a route to relieving premature satiation, an under-addressed barrier to nutritional recovery.

name: Thailand-RIS
title: BetterSweet: Reimagining Sweeteners through Mogroside Pathway Reconstruction
abstract: Novel low-calorie and high-intensity natural sweeteners are needed to address the global overconsumption of sugar that leads to severe health consequences. Monk fruit, or Siraitia grosvenorii, belongs to the cucumber family (Cucurbitaceae), which is native to southern China. It has a special metabolic pathway that produces Mogrosides, a group of triterpene glycosides. The final product of this pathway is Mogroside V, a compound 200-400 times sweeter than table sugar with no calories. However, the production of Monk Fruit remains limited by slow growth and restricted cultivation. Our project aims to reconstruct key steps of the Mogroside biosynthetic pathway in Nicotiana benthamiana, a fast-growing and easily engineered plant host. By establishing an alternative plant-based production system, we hope to make natural sweeteners more accessible, scalable, and environmentally sustainable.

name: UFRGS-Brazil
title: 2,4-Detector: development of a fluorescent biosensor for detecting 2,4-D herbicide in agricultural systems
abstract: The widespread use of 2,4-D in soybean farms causes herbicide drift, threatening neighboring crops. In southern Brazil’s Campanha Gaúcha, this drift devastates viticulture. Containing the issue requires proving contamination, currently a major bottleneck since existing tests demand expensive HPLC equipment, trained personnel, and long-distance sample shipping. To solve this, and guided by consultations with farmers, experts, and technicians, our project developed a portable fluorescent biosensor for 2,4-D. Utilizing the naturally occurring regulatory pair CadR/pCadA, our system recognizes the herbicide and induces an RNA aptamer to emit fluorescence. To optimize this interaction, we employed structural bioinformatics, integrating structure prediction, molecular docking, and dynamics simulations. The mechanism operates entirely within a cell-free system to ensure biosafety and containment. Paired with custom field-reading hardware and a digital reporting forum, 2,4-Detector provides a fast, cost-effective, on-site tool for immediate agricultural monitoring.

name: UM-Macau
title: Guarding the Fridge: A Molecular Photocontrolled Biosensing Toolkit Discriminating Viable Listeria monocytogenes
abstract: Listeria monocytogenes is a major foodborne pathogen capable of proliferating at refrigeration temperatures, posing significant risks to food safety and public health. To enable rapid detection of viable Listeria, we developed a dual-input AND-gate biosensing platform targeting Listeriolysin O (LLO), a virulence factor secreted only by living pathogenic cells. LLO-mediated membrane disruption serves as the first input, while a blue-light-responsive LOV system provides the second input, triggering split-sfGFP complementation or TEV-dependent reporter activation for signal amplification. By integrating fluorescence-based sensing with mathematical modeling, our system enables sensitive quantification of viable bacteria while distinguishing live cells from dead contaminants. Designed with input from food safety stakeholders, the platform is modular, portable, user-friendly, and capable of delivering results within one day, offering a practical solution for real-time food safety surveillance.

name: Zhulu-Union
title: Persephone: PresERvation and Shelf-life Extension of fruits through PostHarvest Optimization by multi-eNgineered Enzymes
abstract:
Persephone is a modular postharvest fruit preservation project targeting ethylene-driven ripening, oxidative damage, and fungal infection. It integrates four modules: ACC deaminase to reduce ethylene biosynthesis, ethylene receptor inhibitory peptides to interfere with ethylene signaling, MnSOD to scavenge superoxide radicals, and chitinase to inhibit fungal growth. ACCD and MnSOD are fused with the cell-penetrating peptide BP100 to improve access to intracellular substrates.
Through computational screening and experimental validation, we combined functional components ACCD–BP100, MnSOD–BP100, B03, and chitinase in a chitosan matrix. Under the tested conditions, this formulation delayed banana peel yellowing by approximately three days and showed less visible mold growth than the 1-MCP treatment group.
The intended product is a powder containing no live microorganisms, reconstituted before use and applied as a spray within existing postharvest workflows.It complements the cold chain, particularly during long-distance fruit transportation and at stages with insufficient cold-chain coverage.
